9	## 1. Product summary
10	
11	### 1.1 Core loop
12	1. User photographs every clothing item, pair of shoes, bag and piece of jewellery they own.
13	2. AI tags each item (category, colors, pattern, fabric, formality, season, style).
14	3. User picks an **anchor item** ("I want to wear this dress").
15	4. App returns 3 complete outfits (shoes, bag, jewellery, outerwear if needed) **using only items the user owns**, plus hairstyle and makeup suggestions and a "gap" suggestion for anything missing.
16	5. User gives feedback (like / dislike / "I wore this"); the app learns their style over time.

18	### 1.2 Feature roadmap (build in this order)
19	| # | Feature | In this spec |
20	|---|---|---|
21	| F1 | Wardrobe capture + AI tagging + closet browser | Full detail |
22	| F2 | **Anchor-item outfit builder** | Full detail |
23	| F3 | Feedback + wear log + style profile (learning) | Full detail |
24	| F4 | Occasion mode (venue lookup, day/night, companions) | Outline (Section 15) |
25	| F5 | Hair/makeup references, gap shopping links, virtual try-on | Outline (Section 15) |
26	
27	**v1 ship target = F1 + F2 + F3.** F4/F5 come after real users have tested v1.

29	### 1.3 Non-goals for v1
30	- No native iOS/Android app (PWA only; wrap with Capacitor later if needed).
31	- No fine-tuning or model training. "Learning" = feedback-driven re-ranking + a text style profile.
32	- No social features, no marketplace, no virtual try-on.
33	- No payments in v1 (add Stripe after beta; see Section 13.5).
34	
35	### 1.4 Guiding principles
36	1. **The LLM chooses from a shortlist; code does everything deterministic.** The LLM may only return item IDs that exist in the shortlist it was given. Validate every output.
37	2. **Tag once, cache forever.** Never re-tag an item unless the user asks.
38	3. **Everything is logged** (model, prompt version, latency, cost) so outputs can be replayed and evaluated.
39	4. **Evals before polish.** The eval harness (Section 11) is built in Milestone 4, before the UI is pretty.

Next is M1: the database migrations with RLS, the private storage bucket, Supabase helpers and magic-link login. It needs a Supabase project (URL, anon key and service-role key) to verify against. If you'd rather not set one up yet, I can write the migrations and tests against the local Supabase CLI instead, which needs Docker. Which do you want?

Turn 2

discuss what is supabase ? whatARE we using it for ?
Claude's response

Supabase is an open-source "backend in a box" built on top of PostgreSQL. Instead of writing and hosting your own server, database, login system and file storage, Supabase gives you all of them as one managed service with a free tier. It's often described as an open-source alternative to Firebase, but it uses a normal SQL database.

What we use it for in Closet

The spec uses three of its parts:

1. Auth (login) - Handles sign-up and login with an email magic link, so there are no passwords to build or store. - Each user gets an ID (auth.uid()). Every table in the app points back to it. - Later it can add Google sign-in.

2. Postgres database - Holds everything structured: the items (each garment or jewellery piece and its AI tags), outfit_sets, outfits, feedback_events, wear_log, style_profiles and llm_calls. - The vector extension is enabled for the future image-similarity feature. v1 doesn't use it.

3. Storage (files) - A private wardrobe bucket holds the photos: original, cutout and thumbnail for each item. - Photos are served to the browser through short-lived signed URLs, never public links.

Row Level Security (RLS)

This is the main reason the spec picks Supabase. RLS is a database rule such as "a row is only visible if user_id = auth.uid()". Even if our app code has a bug, the database refuses to show one user's wardrobe to another. The same idea applies to storage: you can only touch files under your own {user_id}/ folder. That matters here because wardrobe photos are personal and may show faces or bedrooms.

How it fits with the rest of the stack

  • Browser: uses the public anon key. RLS limits what that key can do.
  • Our API routes (server only): can use the service-role key, which bypasses RLS. It's needed for things like writing llm_calls and deleting an account. It must never reach the browser.
  • Anthropic API: completely separate. Supabase only stores data. It does no AI.
  • Vercel: hosts the Next.js app. Supabase hosts the data.

What it costs us

  • Free tier: enough for development and a small beta.
  • Setup: it needs a staging project and a production project (Section 13.2).
  • Local option: you can run a copy on your own machine with the Supabase CLI and Docker, so M1 can be built and tested without a cloud project.

Supabase is a good fit here for three reasons: 1. Auth, database and file storage are all in one place. 2. Per-user privacy is enforced by the database. 3. We avoid building and hosting a backend ourselves.

The trade-off is some lock-in to its conventions. Because it's plain Postgres, though, moving away later is realistic.

For M1, do you want to create a cloud Supabase project, or use the local Docker setup?

Turn 3

so what all is being stored over cloud here ? Where is the global database being managed ?
Claude's response

Four services hold data in the cloud, and the Supabase project is the one that holds user data.

What's stored where

Supabase (cloud, hosted on AWS by Supabase) - Postgres database: - Every user's account (email, user ID). - Item tags, outfits, feedback, wear log and style profile. - The llm_calls cost log. - Storage bucket wardrobe: the actual photos (original, cutout, thumbnail), in per-user folders.

Vercel (cloud) - Hosts only the app code and runs the API routes. It stores no user data. - It holds the environment variables (API keys) as secrets.

Anthropic (cloud) - Receives item photos and tags for each tagging or outfit call and returns the result. - The spec treats it as a processor, not a store. Whether Anthropic retains API inputs depends on its data-retention terms. Check them before you promise users anything in the privacy policy.

GitHub (cloud) - Holds code only, with no user data. Secrets stay out of the repo through .gitignore and the host's env settings.

In the user's browser (not cloud) - Background removal runs locally via WASM. - Images are resized and stripped of EXIF before upload. - The installed PWA caches its own app files.

There's no single "global database"

Each environment gets its own isolated Supabase project:

  • Local: a Docker copy on your machine, or a dev project.
  • Staging: used by Vercel preview deploys.
  • Production: real users only.

Within a project, all users share the same tables, with RLS keeping their rows separate. There's no shared data across projects, and staging data never touches production.

Who manages it

  • Supabase runs the servers, backups and uptime. You don't administer a database server.
  • You own the project and the schema. The schema is managed as SQL migration files in supabase/migrations/, applied with supabase db push, so it's version-controlled and reproducible.
  • You hold the keys. The service-role key can read all users' data, so it lives only in server env vars.

If you'd rather not store user data in the cloud at all, that would mean a different architecture, which the spec doesn't cover.

Turn 4

lets go with the cloud approach. will we need anything for doing google signins -like any permission etc, or is that trivial. can the docker and all be launched on mobile phones as well? ensure that the app is independent of apple / android
Claude's response

Google sign-in

It's not trivial, but it's a one-time setup of about 20 minutes, and you don't need Google's approval to start.

What you need: 1. A Google Cloud project, which is free. 2. An OAuth consent screen. Request only the basic scopes (email, profile, openid). 3. An OAuth Client ID of type "Web application", with Supabase's callback URL as the authorized redirect URI. 4. Paste the Client ID and Secret into the Supabase dashboard under Auth → Providers → Google.

What to know: - Testing mode: while the consent screen is in "Testing", only test users you list (up to 100) can sign in. That's fine for the private beta. - Public launch: you publish the app. With only basic scopes there's no Google security review, but you do need a privacy policy URL and a verified domain. The spec already plans both in M8. - Unverified warning: users see an "unverified app" warning until the consent screen is verified. - Magic link stays: it's the spec's default for v1. Google sign-in is a later add-on, so it doesn't block M1.

Docker on phones

No. Docker is a developer tool and only runs on your computer. You'd only use it for the local Supabase option, and we're skipping that by going cloud. Nothing in this project needs Docker on a phone.

Independence from Apple and Android

The app is a PWA, which is a website that can be installed. That gives you this:

  • No app stores: there's no Apple or Google developer account, no review, no 15–30% fee. Users open the URL and choose "Add to Home Screen".
  • One codebase: the same code runs on iOS, Android and desktop browsers.
  • Camera and photos: these use a standard <input type="file" capture>, which both platforms support.
  • Sign-in: magic link works everywhere. Google sign-in is a Google service, not Apple or Android, and it works in any browser. Don't add "Sign in with Apple". It's only required for native iOS apps that offer other social logins, which doesn't apply here.

Limits to expect: - iOS Safari has weaker PWA support: no automatic install prompt (users add it manually), and tighter background and storage limits. - Push notifications on iOS only work for installed PWAs. - Neither affects v1.

The spec lists a Capacitor wrapper for the app stores as optional and post-validation. Skipping it keeps you independent of both platforms.

Next is M1. Before I can verify against a real database, you need to create a Supabase project and give me the URL, anon key and service-role key. Put them in .env.local, not in chat. Should I write the migrations while you set that up?

Turn 5

is any of what i need charged or is it all free?
Claude's response

Most of it is free to start, but the Anthropic API is pay-per-use and is the one cost you can't avoid. My pricing details come from memory and may be out of date, so check each provider's pricing page before relying on them.

Free

Service Free tier Catch
GitHub Free for private repos None
Google Cloud (OAuth sign-in) Free for basic sign-in You need an account, which may ask for a card
Next.js, Tailwind, shadcn, Vitest and the other libraries Open source None
Sentry, Langfuse (both optional) Free tiers Capped usage

Free with limits

Supabase - Free plan: about 500 MB of database, about 1 GB of file storage, and a monthly user cap. - Free projects pause after about a week of inactivity. - There are no automatic backups, and the free tier doesn't come with production-grade support. - You need a separate project for staging and for production. The free plan has historically limited how many projects you get, so you may need one project to start and a second later. - Photos are the main storage use. A thumbnail plus a resized original is roughly 150–300 KB per item. 1 GB therefore holds a few thousand items, which is enough for a small beta. - The paid Pro plan is about $25/month. Plan on it before public launch, mainly for backups and no pausing.

Vercel - The Hobby plan is free, but it's restricted to non-commercial use. - Once you charge users or run it as a business, you need Pro, about $20/month. - Function time limits are also tighter on Hobby, and the spec's 60s outfit route is near that limit.

Paid, usage-based

Anthropic API - This has no free tier. You prepay credits and set a monthly spend limit in the Console. - Cost scales with use, mainly images tagged and outfit sets generated. - The spec's .env sets a global daily cap of $20 (GLOBAL_DAILY_SPEND_CAP_USD=20), which you can change. - Tagging uses the cheap Haiku model, so it's much cheaper than composing outfits. - I can't give a reliable per-user number now. Once M3 and M5 are running, llm_calls will show the real cost per user.

Paid, optional or later

  • Custom domain: about $10–15/year. It's required for the M8 launch but not for development, since Vercel gives you a free .vercel.app address.
  • Google Places and OpenWeather (F4): post-v1, usage-based with some free allowance.
  • Stripe (payments): no monthly fee, but it takes a percentage of each charge. That's post-beta.
  • Apple and Google developer accounts: not needed, because we're a PWA.

Realistic cost

  • Building and a private beta: $0 for infrastructure, plus a small Anthropic top-up. $5–10 of credit is enough to build and test, but I can't promise that figure.
  • Public launch: roughly $45/month fixed (Supabase Pro plus Vercel Pro) plus Anthropic usage, which should be covered by what users pay once payments are added.

To start M1 you need three free signups: Supabase, Anthropic (with a small prepaid balance and a spend limit) and Google Cloud later for sign-in. Start with Supabase.

Turn 6

every user will use their own api key right ?
Claude's response

No. As the spec is written, you hold one Anthropic API key, it lives only on the server, and every user's requests go through it. Users never see a key, and their requests are billed to your account.

What the spec does

  • The key sits in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, which is a server-side environment variable on Vercel. The browser never calls Anthropic (Section 4.2 rule).
  • Because you pay for everyone, the spec adds cost protection:
  • Per-user daily limits: DAILY_TAG_LIMIT=60 and DAILY_OUTFIT_LIMIT=30.
  • A global daily spend cap of $20 across all users.
  • An llm_calls table logging the cost of each call, so you can see cost per user.
  • Because you carry the cost, the spec plans a free tier of 30 items and 5 outfit sets a week. Paid plans via Stripe come after the beta.

Why not per-user keys

Making each user bring their own key (BYOK) is possible, but it's a poor fit for this app: - Consumer users don't have Anthropic accounts, and asking for an API key would stop most of them signing up. - You'd have to store each key safely, which is a security risk. - You'd lose control over which model and prompt version run.

BYOK suits developer tools. It's not what a consumer app should do.

Your decision

If you don't want to carry the cost, there are two other routes. Both change the spec: - Charge users through subscriptions, which the spec already plans for post-beta. - Cap free use hard so your exposure stays small. The spec already does this with the limits above.

For a 10–20 person beta, the default is fine. You pay a few dollars at most, and the caps stop anyone running up the bill. Should I keep the spec's server-key design?

give me a guide on how to do the SUPABASE part .
Claude's response

Supabase setup guide

1. Create an account

  1. Go to supabase.com and click Start your project.
  2. Sign in with GitHub or email.

2. Create the project

  1. Click New project. If asked, create an Organization first, using any name and the Free plan.
  2. Fill in:
  3. Name: closet-dev. Use a separate project later for staging and production.
  4. Database password: click Generate and save it in a password manager. You can't view it again later.
  5. Region: pick the one closest to your users. If they're in India, choose Mumbai (ap-south-1), because the region can't be changed later.
  6. Click Create new project and wait 1–2 minutes.

3. Get the three keys

  1. In the left sidebar, open Project Settings (gear icon) → API Keys. On some dashboards this is under API.
  2. Copy these into .env.local:
.env.local variable Where to find it
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL Project URL (https://xxxx.supabase.co). It may be under Settings → API or Data API.
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY The anon / public key. Newer projects call it the Publishable key (sb_publishable_...).
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY The service_role key. Newer projects call it the Secret key (sb_secret_...).

Supabase has been moving from the older anon/service_role names to publishable/secret names, so your dashboard may show either. Both work the same way here. If you see both, I'd use the new publishable/secret keys, but I haven't confirmed your dashboard's current layout, so use whichever it shows.

The service-role/secret key is the dangerous one. It bypasses all row-level security and can read every user's data. Never paste it in chat, never commit it, and never put it in a variable starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_.

4. Set up login (for magic links)

  1. Go to Authentication → Sign In / Providers and check that Email is enabled.
  2. Go to Authentication → URL Configuration:
  3. Site URL: http://localhost:3000
  4. Redirect URLs: add http://localhost:3000/**
  5. You'll add the Vercel preview and production URLs later.

Email limit: Supabase's built-in email sender is rate-limited, so only a handful of magic-link emails are allowed per hour. That's fine for solo testing. For a beta you'd add a custom SMTP provider under Authentication → SMTP settings.

5. Tell me when you're done

You don't need to create tables or the storage bucket. I'll write those as SQL migrations. To apply them I need one more thing from you, and there are two ways: - A. Supabase CLI (preferred, reproducible). Run npx supabase login, then npx supabase link --project-ref <your-ref>. The project ref is the xxxx in your project URL. It will ask for the database password from step 2. - B. Paste into the SQL Editor: I give you the migration files and you run them in the dashboard. It's slower and easier to get out of sync with the repo.

For the CLI login, type ! npx supabase login in the prompt so it runs in this session. It opens a browser for approval.

Turn 10

what is this magic link thing
Claude's response

A magic link is a way to log in without a password.

How it works

  1. The user types their email on the login page and taps Send link.
  2. The app emails them a unique, one-time link.
  3. They open the email and tap the link.
  4. It opens the app, already signed in. A session is stored in their browser, so they stay logged in on that device.

The link is the proof of identity. Only someone with access to that inbox can use it.

Why the spec uses it

  • No passwords to build or store: no reset flow, no leaked-password risk, and nothing to forget.
  • Quick to sign up: one field, with no separate account creation step. A new email creates the account automatically.
  • Works on any device: it's just a link, which suits an installable web app.

Things to know

  • Short lifetime: links expire quickly (about an hour by default) and work once.
  • Email dependency: if the email is slow or lands in spam, the user is stuck. That's why I mentioned the built-in sender's rate limit and a custom SMTP provider for the beta.
  • PWA quirk: on iPhones, tapping the link in the Mail app can open Safari instead of the installed home-screen app, which can look like the login "didn't carry over". It's a known annoyance. A six-digit code the user types in is a common fix, and Supabase supports that too. We can add it if testers hit this.
  • Google sign-in: it's the alternative we discussed, and it's a later add-on.

I haven't looked at what's in .env.local since you opened it. Let me know when the Supabase values are filled in.

In the Supabase dashboard, not in your code or .env.local.

Where

  1. Open your project at supabase.com/dashboard and select closet-dev.
  2. In the left sidebar, click Authentication.
  3. Under Configuration, click URL Configuration. The labels may differ slightly in the current dashboard.

What to enter

  • Site URL: http://localhost:3000 This is the default address Supabase redirects to when it has nothing more specific, and the base for links in emails.
  • Redirect URLs: click Add URL and enter http://localhost:3000/** This is the allow-list of addresses Supabase will send a user back to after login. The ** wildcard covers any path, such as the /auth/callback page I'll build in M1. A redirect to an address not on the list is blocked.

Click Save.

Later

When you deploy, add the live addresses to the same Redirect URLs list: - the Vercel preview pattern, for example https://*-yourteam.vercel.app/** - your production domain, for example https://yourdomain.com/**

Change the Site URL to the production domain when you launch. Staging and production each have their own Supabase project, so each project has its own list.

Matching .env.local

NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 in .env.local should match the Site URL. It already does. My login code reads it to build the link users return to.

import { createServerClient } from "@supabase/ssr";
import { createClient as createSupabaseClient } from "@supabase/supabase-js";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";

/** Session-bound client for server components and route handlers (RLS applies). */
export async function createClient() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  return createServerClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!,
    {
      cookies: {
        getAll: () => cookieStore.getAll(),
        setAll: (toSet) => {
          try {
            toSet.forEach(({ name, value, options }) => cookieStore.set(name, value, options));
          } catch {
            // Called from a Server Component; middleware refreshes the session instead.
          }
        },
      },
    },
  );
}

/** Service-role client. Bypasses RLS. Server-only: never import from client code. */
export function createAdminClient() {
  return createSupabaseClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY!,
    { auth: { persistSession: false, autoRefreshToken: false } },
  );
}
EOF
cat > src/lib/supabase/middleware.ts <<'EOF'
import { createServerClient } from "@supabase/ssr";
import { NextResponse, type NextRequest } from "next/server";

const PUBLIC_PATHS = ["/login", "/auth", "/privacy", "/terms"];

/** Refreshes the session cookie and redirects logged-out users to /login. */
export async function updateSession(request: NextRequest) {
  let response = NextResponse.next({ request });

  const supabase = createServerClient(
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!,
    {
      cookies: {
        getAll: () => request.cookies.getAll(),
        setAll: (toSet) => {
          toSet.forEach(({ name, value }) => request.cookies.set(name, value));
          response = NextResponse.next({ request });
          toSet.forEach(({ name, value, options }) => response.cookies.set(name, value, options));
        },
      },
    },
  );

  const {
    data: { user },
  } = await supabase.auth.getUser();

  const path = request.nextUrl.pathname;
  const isPublic = PUBLIC_PATHS.some((p) => path === p || path.startsWith(`${p}/`));

  if (!user && !isPublic) {
    const url = request.nextUrl.clone();
    url.pathname = "/login";
    return NextResponse.redirect(url);
  }
  if (user && path === "/login") {
    const url = request.nextUrl.clone();
    url.pathname = "/closet";
    return NextResponse.redirect(url);
  }
  return response;
}
EOF

// Integration test against the real Supabase project in .env.local.
// Run with `npm run test:rls`. Creates two throwaway users and deletes them afterwards.
import { config } from "dotenv";
import { randomUUID } from "crypto";
import { afterAll, beforeAll, describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { createClient, type SupabaseClient } from "@supabase/supabase-js";

config({ path: ".env.local" });

const url = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!;
const anon = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY!;
const admin = createClient(url, process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY!, {
  auth: { persistSession: false },
});

type TestUser = { id: string; client: SupabaseClient };
const password = `Pw-${randomUUID()}`;
const users: TestUser[] = [];
let itemA: string;
let outfitA: string;
const fileA = () => `${users[0].id}/${itemA}/original.jpg`;

async function makeUser(): Promise<TestUser> {
  const email = `rls-${randomUUID()}@example.com`;
  const { data, error } = await admin.auth.admin.createUser({ email, password, email_confirm: true });
  if (error) throw error;
  const client = createClient(url, anon, { auth: { persistSession: false } });
  const { error: signInError } = await client.auth.signInWithPassword({ email, password });
  if (signInError) throw signInError;
  return { id: data.user.id, client };
}

beforeAll(async () => {
  users.push(await makeUser(), await makeUser());
  const [a] = users;

  const item = await a.client
    .from("items")
    .insert({ user_id: a.id, image_path: "x", category: "tshirt", slot: "top" })
    .select("id")
    .single();
  expect(item.error).toBeNull();
  itemA = item.data!.id;

  const set = await a.client.from("outfit_sets").insert({ user_id: a.id }).select("id").single();
  const outfit = await a.client
    .from("outfits")
    .insert({ user_id: a.id, set_id: set.data!.id })
    .select("id")
    .single();
  outfitA = outfit.data!.id;
  await a.client.from("outfit_items").insert({ outfit_id: outfitA, item_id: itemA, slot: "top" });
  await a.client.from("wear_log").insert({ user_id: a.id, item_id: itemA });
  await a.client.from("feedback_events").insert({ user_id: a.id, type: "like", outfit_id: outfitA });
  await a.client.from("style_profiles").insert({ user_id: a.id, summary_text: "secret" });
  await admin.from("llm_calls").insert({ user_id: a.id, purpose: "tag" });

  const up = await a.client.storage
    .from("wardrobe")
    .upload(fileA(), new Blob(["x"], { type: "image/jpeg" }), { contentType: "image/jpeg" });
  expect(up.error).toBeNull();
}, 60_000);

afterAll(async () => {
  await admin.storage.from("wardrobe").remove([fileA()]);
  for (const u of users) await admin.auth.admin.deleteUser(u.id);
});

describe("row isolation", () => {
  const tables = [
    "items",
    "outfit_sets",
    "outfits",
    "outfit_items",
    "wear_log",
    "feedback_events",
    "style_profiles",
  ] as const;

  it.each(tables)("owner sees own rows in %s", async (table) => {
    const { data } = await users[0].client.from(table).select("*");
    expect(data!.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });

  it.each(tables)("other user sees nothing in %s", async (table) => {
    const { data, error } = await users[1].client.from(table).select("*");
    expect(error).toBeNull();
    expect(data).toEqual([]);
  });

  it("other user cannot update or delete someone else's item", async () => {

cat > src/lib/upload/prepare.ts <<'EOF'
"use client";

import imageCompression from "browser-image-compression";
import { ALLOWED_INPUT_MIME, MAX_LONG_SIDE, MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES } from "@/lib/storage-paths";

const THUMB_SIDE = 320;
const BG_REMOVAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 45_000;

export type Prepared = { original: Blob; thumb: Blob; cutout: Blob | null; cutoutFailed: boolean };

const isHeic = (f: File) =>
  /image\/hei[cf]/i.test(f.type) || /\.hei[cf]$/i.test(f.name);

/** Returns an error message if the file should be rejected before any processing. */
export function checkFile(file: File): string | null {
  if (file.size > MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES) return "Larger than 10 MB";
  if (!ALLOWED_INPUT_MIME.includes(file.type) && !isHeic(file)) return "Not a supported image type";
  return null;
}

async function toJpegSource(file: File): Promise<File> {
  if (!isHeic(file)) return file;
  const { default: heic2any } = await import("heic2any");
  const out = await heic2any({ blob: file, toType: "image/jpeg", quality: 0.9 });
  const blob = Array.isArray(out) ? out[0] : out;
  return new File([blob], file.name.replace(/\.hei[cf]$/i, ".jpg"), { type: "image/jpeg" });
}

/** Re-encoding through a canvas drops EXIF (including GPS) and bakes in orientation. */
const resize = (file: File, side: number, type: "image/jpeg" | "image/png" = "image/jpeg") =>
  imageCompression(file, {
    maxWidthOrHeight: side,
    maxSizeMB: 1,
    fileType: type,
    useWebWorker: true,
    preserveExif: false,
    initialQuality: 0.85,
  });

async function removeBackground(source: Blob): Promise<Blob> {
  const { removeBackground: run } = await import("@imgly/background-removal");
  const result = await Promise.race([
    run(source, { output: { format: "image/png" } }),
    new Promise<never>((_, reject) =>
      setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("background removal timed out")), BG_REMOVAL_TIMEOUT_MS),
    ),
  ]);
  return result;
}

export async function prepareImage(file: File, opts: { removeBg: boolean }): Promise<Prepared> {
  const source = await toJpegSource(file);
  const original = await resize(source, MAX_LONG_SIDE);
  const thumb = await resize(new File([original], "o.jpg", { type: "image/jpeg" }), THUMB_SIDE);

  let cutout: Blob | null = null;
  let cutoutFailed = false;
  if (opts.removeBg) {
    try {
      cutout = await removeBackground(original);
    } catch {
      cutoutFailed = true; // fall back to the plain photo
    }
  }
  return { original, thumb, cutout, cutoutFailed };
}
EOF

Upload them through the app, on the Add items page.

  1. Make sure the dev server is running (npm run dev, or it may still be running in the background).
  2. Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with your magic link if you aren't already.

Testing on a phone

The phone has to reach your computer's dev server:

  1. Put the phone on the same Wi-Fi as your computer.
  2. Find your computer's LAN IP (run hostname -I) and open http://<that-ip>:3000 on the phone. The dev server may need to listen on all interfaces. If it won't load, run npm run dev -- -H 0.0.0.0.
  3. Add http://<that-ip>:3000/** to the Redirect URLs in Supabase (Authentication → URL Configuration), or the magic link won't bring you back to the right place.

Possible camera problem: some phone browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS, not plain http:// over the LAN. If Take photo doesn't work, use Choose photos instead. That opens the photo library, which should still work. Real phone testing is easier from a Vercel preview deployment, which has HTTPS.

If you only want to check that the pipeline works, upload a few photos from your computer first. Photos of single items on a plain background work best. Avoid selfies, since the tagger will reject those in M3.

cat > src/lib/limits.ts <<'EOF'
import { createAdminClient } from "@/lib/supabase/server";

export type LlmPurpose = "tag" | "compose" | "extras" | "judge";

export class LimitError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "LimitError";
  }
}

const num = (v: string | undefined, fallback: number) => {
  const n = Number(v);
  return Number.isFinite(n) && v !== undefined && v !== "" ? n : fallback;
};

const startOfUtcDay = () => {
  const d = new Date();
  d.setUTCHours(0, 0, 0, 0);
  return d.toISOString();
};

/** Daily per-user call limit for a purpose; only tag and compose are user-limited. */
export function dailyLimitFor(purpose: LlmPurpose): number | null {
  if (purpose === "tag") return num(process.env.DAILY_TAG_LIMIT, 60);
  if (purpose === "compose") return num(process.env.DAILY_OUTFIT_LIMIT, 30);
  return null;
}

/** Throws LimitError (with a user-friendly message) if the user or the whole app is over a cap. */
export async function enforceLimits(userId: string, purpose: LlmPurpose) {
  const admin = createAdminClient();
  const since = startOfUtcDay();

  const userLimit = dailyLimitFor(purpose);
  if (userLimit !== null) {
    const { count } = await admin
      .from("llm_calls")
      .select("id", { count: "exact", head: true })
      .eq("user_id", userId)
      .eq("purpose", purpose)
      .eq("ok", true)
      .gte("created_at", since);
    if ((count ?? 0) >= userLimit) {
      throw new LimitError("You've reached today's limit. Please try again tomorrow.");
    }
  }

  const cap = num(process.env.GLOBAL_DAILY_SPEND_CAP_USD, 20);
  const { data } = await admin.from("llm_calls").select("cost_usd").gte("created_at", since);
  const spent = (data ?? []).reduce((sum, r) => sum + Number(r.cost_usd ?? 0), 0);
  if (spent >= cap) {
    throw new LimitError("The service is busy right now. Please try again later.");
  }
}

 * without touching callers. See DECISIONS.md.
 */
export function getAnthropicKey(_userId: string): string {
  void _userId;
  const key = process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY;
  if (!key || key.startsWith("your-")) throw new Error("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not configured");
  return key;
}

/** USD per million tokens [input, output]. Override with MODEL_PRICES_JSON='{"model":[in,out]}'. */
const DEFAULT_PRICES: Record<string, [number, number]> = {
  "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001": [1, 5],
};
const FALLBACK_PRICE: [number, number] = [3, 15];

export function costUsd(model: string, inputTokens: number, outputTokens: number): number {
  let overrides: Record<string, [number, number]> = {};
  try {

  } catch {}
  const [pin, pout] = overrides[model] ?? DEFAULT_PRICES[model] ?? FALLBACK_PRICE;
  return (inputTokens * pin + outputTokens * pout) / 1_000_000;

import { CATEGORIES_BY_SLOT, CategorySchema } from "@/lib/styling/taxonomy";
import { METAL_TONES, PATTERNS, SEASONS } from "@/lib/ai/tagger";

const ColorSchema = z.object({

});

/** Fields a user may edit. Anything omitted is left unchanged. */
export const EditableTags = z
  .object({
    slot: SlotSchema,
    category: CategorySchema,
    subcategory: z.string().max(60).nullable(),
    colors: z.array(ColorSchema).min(1).max(4),

    formality: z.number().int().min(1).max(5),

    statement_level: z.number().int().min(1).max(5),
    metal_tone: z.enum(METAL_TONES).nullable(),
    style_tags: z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(6),
    occasions: z.array(z.string().max(30)).max(6),
  })
  .partial();
export type EditableTags = z.infer<typeof EditableTags>;

export const PatchItemRequest = EditableTags.extend({ confirm: z.boolean().default(true) });

export const categoryMatchesSlot = (slot: string, category: string) =>
  (CATEGORIES_BY_SLOT as Record<string, readonly string[]>)[slot]?.includes(category) ?? false;

"use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { useState } from "react";
import { runPool, tagItem } from "@/lib/upload/pipeline";

/** Retries tagging for items that were uploaded but never tagged (e.g. a failed or limited run). */
export function TagUntagged({ ids }: { ids: string[] }) {
  const router = useRouter();
  const [busy, setBusy] = useState(false);
  const [errors, setErrors] = useState<string[]>([]);

  async function run() {
    setBusy(true);
    setErrors([]);
    const errs: string[] = [];
    await runPool(ids, 3, async (id) => {
      try {
        await tagItem(id);
      } catch (e) {
        errs.push(e instanceof Error ? e.message : "Tagging failed");
      }
    });
    setErrors([...new Set(errs)]);
    setBusy(false);
    router.refresh();
  }

  return (
    <div className="flex flex-col gap-1 rounded-lg border border-amber-400 p-3 text-sm">
      <p>{ids.length} item{ids.length === 1 ? "" : "s"} not tagged yet.</p>
      <button onClick={run} disabled={busy} className="self-start rounded-lg border border-neutral-300 px-3 py-1 disabled:opacity-50">
        {busy ? "Tagging…" : "Tag now"}
      </button>
      {errors.map((e) => (
        <p key={e} role="alert" className="text-red-600">{e}</p>
      ))}
    </div>
  );
}

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { z } from "zod";
import { costUsd } from "@/lib/ai/client";
import { TagResult } from "@/lib/ai/tagger";
import { categoryMatchesSlot, PatchItemRequest } from "@/lib/schemas";

const valid = {
  is_wardrobe_item: true,
  slot: "top",
  category: "tshirt",
  subcategory: "white crew-neck tee",
  colors: [{ name: "white", hex: "#FAFAFA", role: "primary" }],
  pattern: "solid",
  fabric: "cotton",
  formality: 2,
  warmth: 2,
  seasons: ["summer"],
  statement_level: 1,
  style_tags: ["basic"],
  occasions: ["casual"],
  confidence: { slot: 0.99, category: 0.9 },
};

describe("TagResult", () => {
  it("accepts a valid tag", () => {
    expect(TagResult.safeParse(valid).success).toBe(true);
  });
  it("rejects a category that does not belong to the slot", () => {
    expect(TagResult.safeParse({ ...valid, category: "heels" }).success).toBe(false);
  });
  it("rejects bad hex, out-of-range formality and unknown slots", () => {
    expect(TagResult.safeParse({ ...valid, colors: [{ name: "x", hex: "red", role: "primary" }] }).success).toBe(false);
    expect(TagResult.safeParse({ ...valid, formality: 6 }).success).toBe(false);
    expect(TagResult.safeParse({ ...valid, slot: "hat" }).success).toBe(false);
  });
  it("skips the slot/category check for rejected photos", () => {
    expect(TagResult.safeParse({ ...valid, is_wardrobe_item: false, category: "heels" }).success).toBe(true);
  });
  it("converts to a JSON schema usable as a tool input", () => {
    const js = z.toJSONSchema(TagResult) as { type: string; properties: Record<string, unknown> };
    expect(js.type).toBe("object");
    expect(js.properties).toHaveProperty("slot");
  });
});

describe("costUsd", () => {
  it("prices haiku at $1/$5 per million tokens", () => {
    expect(costUsd("claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", 1_000_000, 1_000_000)).toBeCloseTo(6);
  });
  it("uses a conservative fallback for unknown models", () => {
    expect(costUsd("mystery", 1_000_000, 0)).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  });
});

describe("PatchItemRequest / categoryMatchesSlot", () => {
  it("allows partial edits and defaults confirm to true", () => {
    const r = PatchItemRequest.parse({ formality: 4 });
    expect(r.confirm).toBe(true);
    expect(r.formality).toBe(4);
  });
  it("rejects invalid values", () => {
    expect(PatchItemRequest.safeParse({ formality: 9 }).success).toBe(false);
  });
  it("checks category against slot", () => {
    expect(categoryMatchesSlot("onepiece", "saree")).toBe(true);
    expect(categoryMatchesSlot("top", "saree")).toBe(false);
  });
});

The problem

Fix

  1. Go to console.anthropic.com → API Keys → Create Key.
  2. Open .env.local and replace the value on the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= line with the new key. It should start with sk-ant-.
  3. Make sure your Console account has a small prepaid balance and a monthly spend limit.
  4. Tell me when it's done, and I'll rerun the live tagger test. It makes two real calls, a few cents in total.

What's built

  • AI client (src/lib/ai/client.ts):
  • Forced tool-use calls with Zod parsing and one repair retry.
  • The SDK retries up to 2 times on 429 and 5xx errors.
  • Every call is logged to llm_calls with tokens, cost and latency, never image bytes.
  • Spend caps are checked before each call: the daily per-user limit and the global cap.
  • The key comes through one function, getAnthropicKey(userId), so per-user keys stay easy later.
  • Tagger: a versioned prompt (tagger.v1) and the full schema from spec 7.1. A category that doesn't belong to its slot is rejected and repaired.
  • API routes:
  • POST /api/items/[id]/tag runs the tagger.
  • PATCH saves edits, confirms the tags, and logs a tag_correction event for each changed field.
  • DELETE removes the item and its files.
  • Upload flow: each photo is now tagged automatically after upload, three at a time. A photo that isn't clothing is rejected with a clear message and removed.
  • Closet: a "Tag now" button retries any item that failed to tag. A "N need review" link opens the review carousel.
  • Review carousel: swipeable, with editable tags. Fields the AI was less than 60% sure of are highlighted.
  • Tests: 14 unit tests pass. Typecheck, lint and build are clean.

Turn 19

what do you mean rejected phots?
Claude's response

When you upload a photo, the AI first decides whether it shows a wardrobe item. If it doesn't, the app rejects the photo.

What counts as rejected

The tagger's first output field is is_wardrobe_item. It's set to false when the photo is something like: - a selfie or a photo of a person with no clear item - a blurry or very dark photo - a room, a document or a screenshot - a photo with nothing recognisable in it

The spec calls for this (Section 7.1 and the "photo rejected: not a clothing item" flow in Section 10).

What happens to a rejected photo

  1. The upload itself works, so the photo briefly exists in your storage and in the items table.
  2. The tagger says it isn't a wardrobe item.
  3. The app deletes the photo from storage and removes its row.
  4. The upload screen shows that file as failed, with a message like "Photo rejected: ".

So a rejected photo never shows up in your closet.

The choice I made

The spec says to reject non-wardrobe photos, but it doesn't say whether to delete them. I picked automatic deletion because it keeps junk out of the closet, and it means we hold less of your photos, which fits the privacy goal. The downside is that if the AI wrongly rejects a real item, say a hard-to-recognise piece of jewellery, the photo is gone and you have to re-upload it.

Alternatives

  • Keep it, flagged: the photo stays in an "Untagged" state, and "Tag now" retries it. That's safer against false rejections but leaves clutter.
  • Ask first: the app shows "This doesn't look like clothing. Keep it anyway?" That's friendlier but needs a new screen.

Do you want to keep auto-delete, or switch to one of the other two?

Jewellery and shoes

Both are already covered, since they're part of the taxonomy the tagger must choose from: - Shoes: sneakers, heels, flats, sandals, boots, wedges, mojari/juttis. - Jewellery: four slots by body part (neck, ear, wrist, other) with categories like jhumkas, maang tikka, bangles and layered chains.

I've just bumped the prompt to tagger.v2. It now spells out the tricky cases: a shoe or earring pair counts as one item, jewellery always gets a metal tone and a statement level, matching sets (necklace plus earrings in one photo) are flagged with lower confidence, and items shown on a person are tagged as the item only.

Not proven yet. I haven't seen the tagger tag a single real photo, because the Anthropic key is invalid. I don't know its jewellery accuracy. Small, thin jewellery is the hardest case for any vision model at 1024px. The M4 tagging eval, using your labeled photos, is what will measure this. Please include plenty of jewellery and shoes in those 40.

How tagging works

Flow, one photo at a time (three in parallel): 1. In your browser: HEIC is converted to JPEG, the image is resized to 1024px or smaller, and EXIF/location data is stripped. 2. The photo is uploaded to your private Supabase storage, and an items row is created as "untagged". 3. The browser calls POST /api/items/[id]/tag. 4. On the server: the route loads the resized original from storage (not the background-removed cutout) and base64-encodes it. 5. It calls the Anthropic API through src/lib/ai/client.ts. That wrapper checks the daily limits and the global spend cap first. 6. The model is forced to answer through a tool call, so the reply is structured JSON and not free text. 7. The reply is checked against the Zod schema in code, including a rule that the category must belong to the chosen slot. If it fails, the model gets one repair attempt with the exact validation errors. 8. The tags are saved to the row, and the call is logged in llm_calls with tokens, cost and latency, never the image. 9. Fields with confidence under 0.6 are highlighted in the review screen. Your edits are saved and logged as tag_correction events.

Model: Claude Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001), the cheap vision tier. It's set by MODEL_TAGGER in .env.local, so it can be swapped without code changes. The spec's rule is to tag once and cache forever. A photo is never re-tagged unless you ask.

What it sends: one image plus a system prompt containing the taxonomy and rules. It sends no other photos and no information about you.

If Haiku turns out too weak on jewellery, the fix is cheap: point MODEL_TAGGER at a stronger model for a trial run through the eval. Keep in mind that the Anthropic API receives your photos, which is worth stating in the privacy policy.

Turn 22

After every item is tagged, the app runs a pipeline that finds what goes with what. Code first generates only slot-valid pairs (dress with shoes, top with bottom, outfit with earrings) and scores them with deterministic rules for color harmony, formality, season, and neckline-to-jewellery fit. Clearly good and clearly bad pairs are settled there. The uncertain middle band goes to a vision model that judges them in batches and returns a score and a reason. Code then assembles full outfits around each hero piece with a beam search, because pairs that match individually can still clash as a set. A curator model picks the best three to five looks per hero, and a critic model checks them with tools (look at the item image, check a pair, validate an outfit) for 1-2 revision rounds. The results are stored as pair scores, finished looks, and graph stats, which also reveal orphan items and wardrobe gaps. New or edited items only trigger re-scoring of their own pairs, so anchor-item requests become fast lookups instead of fresh LLM calls. follow this
Claude's response

This is a different shape from the spec's M5. Instead of composing outfits on demand, it precomputes a compatibility graph of rule-scored pairs, a vision model for the uncertain ones, beam-searched outfits and a critic. I'll record the change as a decision, then build the first stage, the deterministic pair layer, which the design requires in any case.

Bash: npm i culori 2>&1 | tail -1; npm i -D @types/culori 2>&1 | tail -1; mkdir -p docs && cat > docs/PAIR
npm i culori 2>&1 | tail -1; npm i -D @types/culori 2>&1 | tail -1; mkdir -p docs && cat > docs/PAIRGRAPH.md <<'EOF'
# Compatibility-graph pipeline (replaces SPEC §7.2 on-demand composer)

Decided by the product owner after M3. Outfits are **precomputed**, not composed per request.

## Stages
1. **Pair generation (code).** Only slot-valid pairs (`SLOT_PAIRS` in `slots.ts`): dress+shoes, top+bottom, outfit+earrings, ...
2. **Rule scoring (code).** `pairScore()` = colour harmony, formality, season, style/occasion overlap, neckline-to-jewellery, pattern rule, metal tone. Score ≥ `GOOD` → settled good; ≤ `BAD` (or a hard fail) → settled bad; between → **uncertain**.
3. **Vision judge (LLM, batched).** Only uncertain pairs. Batches of N pairs with both thumbnails; returns `{score, reason}` per pair. Stored with `source='vision'`.
4. **Beam search (code).** Assemble full outfits around each hero piece (dress / onepiece / top+bottom / outerwear). Beam keeps top-K partial outfits by mean pair score + whole-set penalties (too many statement pieces, mixed metals, pattern clash) because individually good pairs can clash as a set.
5. **Curator (LLM).** Picks the best 3–5 looks per hero from the beam finalists; writes title + reasoning.
6. **Critic (LLM with tools).** Tools: `view_item(id)`, `check_pair(a,b)`, `validate_outfit(items)`. 1–2 revision rounds; may replace items, never invent ids.
7. **Store.** `pair_scores`, `looks`, `wardrobe_graph_stats` (orphans = items with no good pair; gaps = slots whose best pairs are weak).

## Incremental updates
Each pair row stores a `fingerprint` (hash of both items' scoring-relevant tags). A new or edited item changes its fingerprint, so only its own pairs are re-scored; looks containing it are marked stale and regenerated. Anchor requests become lookups against `looks` (+ a code swap/fallback when none exist).

## Guardrails kept from the spec
- LLMs only see/return ids from supplied sets; all output is Zod-parsed and re-validated by `validate.ts`.
- Every call goes through `ai/client.ts` (caps, logging). Precompute jobs count toward the global spend cap.
- Hard gates from §11.2 still apply, now measured on stored looks.

## Cost controls (open decisions, defaults chosen)
- Vision judge only on the uncertain band; max `MAX_VISION_PAIRS_PER_RUN` per job (default 150) — the rest stay rule-scored until the next run.
- Hero pieces processed in recency order; critic runs once per hero.

-- Compatibility graph (docs/PAIRGRAPH.md): scored pairs, finished looks, per-user graph stats.

create table pair_scores (
  user_id uuid not null references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  item_a uuid not null references items(id) on delete cascade,   -- item_a < item_b (canonical order)
  item_b uuid not null references items(id) on delete cascade,
  score numeric(4,3) not null,
  band text not null check (band in ('good','bad','uncertain')),
  source text not null check (source in ('rules','vision')),
  reason text,
  fingerprint text not null,            -- hash of both items' scoring tags; mismatch => stale
  model text, prompt_version text,
  updated_at timestamptz default now(),
  primary key (item_a, item_b),
  check (item_a < item_b)
);
create index on pair_scores (user_id, band);
create index on pair_scores (item_b);

create table looks (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id uuid not null references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  hero_item_id uuid not null references items(id) on delete cascade,
  items jsonb not null,                 -- { slot: item_id }
  score numeric(4,3) not null,
  title text, reasoning text,
  critic_notes text,
  stale boolean not null default false, -- set when a member item changes
  model text, prompt_version text,
  created_at timestamptz default now()
);
create index on looks (user_id, hero_item_id) where stale = false;

create table wardrobe_graph_stats (
  user_id uuid primary key references auth.users(id) on delete cascade,
  stats jsonb not null default '{}',    -- { orphans: [item_id], gaps: [{slot, reason}], counts: {...} }
  updated_at timestamptz default now()
);

alter table pair_scores enable row level security;
alter table looks enable row level security;
alter table wardrobe_graph_stats enable row level security;

create policy pair_scores_own on pair_scores for all to authenticated

  with check (
    user_id = (select auth.uid())
    and exists (select 1 from items i where i.id = item_a and i.user_id = (select auth.uid()))

create policy looks_own on looks for all to authenticated

create policy graph_stats_own on wardrobe_graph_stats for all to authenticated
  using (user_id = (select auth.uid())) with check (user_id = (select auth.uid()));

I've started on your pipeline, and stage 1 (the rule-based pair layer) is built and committed. Stages 2–7 aren't built.

What's built

  • Design record: docs/PAIRGRAPH.md describes all seven stages. DECISIONS.md notes that this replaces the spec's on-demand composer, so /api/outfits/anchor becomes a lookup of stored looks.
  • Slot-valid pairs: slots.ts only pairs things that can be worn together. A dress never pairs with a separate top or bottom, and jewellery isn't paired with other jewellery. The spec's slot plan table (Section 6.1) is encoded here too.
  • Colour: color.ts uses culori and the spec's rules: neutrals are safe, analogous colours score well, loud colours clash. The metal-versus-outfit-warmth rule for jewellery is in too.
  • Pair scoring: pairScore.ts combines colour, formality (hard fail above a 1-step gap, 2 for bags and jewellery), season, style/occasion overlap, the two-patterns rule, and neckline-versus-necklace. Each pair comes out as good, bad or uncertain. The thresholds are in one config file.
  • Incremental updates: each pair stores a fingerprint of both items' tags. Changing one item re-scores only that item's pairs, and uncertainPairs() picks out the ones for the vision judge.
  • Storage schema: pair_scores, looks and wardrobe_graph_stats, with RLS, in migration file 5. It's written but not applied.
  • Checks: 38 unit tests pass, with 92.7% coverage on the engine (spec target is 90%). The tests caught a real bug, a neckline pattern that missed "turtleneck", which I fixed. Typecheck and lint are clean.

Still to build, in order

  1. Vision judge for uncertain pairs, in batches
  2. Beam search over whole outfits
  3. Curator model
  4. Critic model with its three tools
  5. Storing results and graph stats (orphans and gaps)
  6. Hooking into upload and edit so changes trigger re-scoring

Two things to know

  • Vision-judge cost is the main risk. A closet with 100 items has thousands of slot-valid pairs. Only the uncertain middle band goes to the model, and I capped it at 150 pairs per run (MAX_VISION_PAIRS_PER_RUN). That number is my guess and needs tuning against real costs. These jobs also use the global spend cap.
  • The rule thresholds are untested. The 0.75 and 0.4 band edges are my first guesses. Whether the "good" band is trustworthy will only show with your wardrobe and the M4 eval cases.

What it takes

All model calls go through one file, src/lib/ai/client.ts, so I'd make that file provider-agnostic:

  1. Add a provider setting, for example AI_PROVIDER=gemini|anthropic, and keep getAnthropicKey as the single place keys are resolved.
  2. Add a Gemini adapter that sends the image and prompt and forces structured JSON output, using Gemini's own mechanism in place of Anthropic tool use.
  3. Convert my Zod schemas to the schema format Gemini accepts. Gemini supports a narrower subset of JSON Schema, so some constructs (the optional fields, the per-field confidence map) may need adjusting.
  4. Add Gemini model names to the env settings and to the cost table.

The tagger, the review screen and the rest of the pipeline stay the same. It's about an hour of work, and I'd keep the Zod validation and repair retry as they are.

Things to weigh

  • Quality is untested. The tagger prompt was written for Claude. Gemini may do better or worse on jewellery and Indian garments, and I can't tell without your labeled photos. The M4 tagging eval is exactly the tool for comparing the two.
  • Privacy, which matters here. The spec promises that wardrobe photos are never used for training. As I remember it, Google's free Gemini API tier may use your inputs to improve its products, while the paid tier does not. Check Google's current terms before uploading personal photos, or before promising users anything.
  • Free tier limits. Gemini's free tier has rate limits that could slow a 20-photo batch. Check its current limits.
  • Pipeline stages 5 and 6 (curator and critic) rely on tool use. Gemini supports function calling, but I haven't tested that path.

My suggestion

Build the provider switch. Anthropic stays the default if you have a working key, and Gemini becomes an option you can compare in the eval. It also helps the later per-user-key idea, since a user might bring either provider.

Turn 24

can we locally train a VLM for tagging ?
Claude's response

Yes, you can, and it's more realistic than it sounds. Training from scratch is a bad idea, but there are three levels of "local", and the first two are cheap.

Option 1: run an existing open VLM locally (no training)

Open vision-language models can read a clothing photo and return JSON tags. Families like Qwen-VL, Gemma and SmolVLM are the usual candidates. I'm going from memory on current model names and sizes, so check what's newest before choosing. You'd run one through a local server such as Ollama or vLLM, behind the same provider switch we discussed for Gemini. It costs nothing per call, and photos never leave your machine, which fits the privacy goal. The catches: - Hardware: a usable model needs a GPU with roughly 8–16 GB of VRAM. On CPU only, each photo would take many seconds to minutes. - Quality: small models are weaker on fine distinctions, such as jhumkas versus drops or the exact colour hex. Whether that's good enough is something the eval will show. - Structured output: these servers can constrain output to a JSON schema, so the tags would still conform.

Option 2: fine-tune one with LoRA

This is where "training" comes in. You take an open VLM and teach it your taxonomy and labelling style on your own labeled photos. It usually helps most on consistency, such as always picking valid categories, and on regional items the base model handles poorly. Rough requirements: - Several hundred to a few thousand labeled photos. The 40 we planned for the eval aren't enough to train on, and they must stay out of training so the eval stays honest. - A GPU with enough memory for LoRA, a few hours of compute, and some training code. - The corrections you make in the review screen are exactly the training data. Every tag_correction event is a labelled example, which is why the spec logs them.

Option 3: train from scratch

Not realistic. It takes millions of images and serious compute, and it would be worse than Option 1.

Where this leaves the spec

The spec sets this aside for v1: no fine-tuning, and only consider a smaller open model if API cost or latency becomes a real problem, with 10k or more tagged images. There's a deployment issue too. Your app runs on Vercel, which can't host a GPU model. A local model would work for development, but a deployed app would need a separate GPU server or a hosted inference service.

My suggestion

  1. Build the provider switch (Anthropic, Gemini, local) so the tagger isn't tied to one vendor.
  2. Run the tagging eval to compare them on your labeled photos.
  3. Collect corrections as you use the app. Fine-tune later only if a local model is close to good enough and the data is there.

What GPU do you have, and how much VRAM? That decides whether Option 1 is practical on your machine.

Turn 25

if someone finnaly ha to be able to use this as a phone application which options would you recommend and why ?
Claude's response

I'd recommend a staged path: keep the installable web app (PWA) now, wrap it with Capacitor if you need the app stores, and consider a full rebuild only if real users demand it.

The options

1. PWA (what we're building) - For: one codebase, no app-store accounts, fees or review, and instant updates. It also matches your earlier request to stay independent of Apple and Android. - Against: on iPhone, installing is manual ("Add to Home Screen"), and Safari is stricter about storage, background work and push notifications. It isn't discoverable in app stores, and some users won't trust an app that isn't in one.

2. Capacitor wrapper (the spec's own plan) - It puts the same web app inside a native shell, so it can be published to the Apple App Store and Google Play. You reuse nearly all your code, and you gain native plugins for the camera, photo library and push notifications. - For: the fastest route to the stores, and it fixes the iOS PWA weaknesses. - Against: it's still a web view, so animations won't feel perfectly native, and you'll maintain the shell. Apple sometimes rejects apps that are just a wrapped website, so you'd want real native features such as the camera and push notifications. Both stores need developer accounts. I believe Apple's is about $99 a year and Google's a one-time fee of about $25, but check the current prices.

3. React Native / Expo - For: a truly native feel, better camera and gallery handling, and strong offline support. - Against: it's a large rewrite of the interface. The backend (Supabase, API routes, styling engine) could be reused, and some of the TypeScript logic could be shared, but all the screens would be rebuilt.

4. Fully native (Swift and Kotlin) - Best performance and deepest platform access, but you'd build and maintain two apps. It isn't justified for this product.

Why this order

  • The product is a camera, a grid, forms and image cards. A web view handles that well, so there's no early need for native rendering.
  • The riskiest unknown is whether people want the product, not whether it feels native. A PWA costs nothing to ship and update while you learn that.
  • Because the AI and styling logic live on the server, a wrapper or a rebuild would reuse the entire backend. Nothing we're building now gets thrown away.

What I'd do now to keep the options open

  • Keep all business logic in server routes and the pure styling/ code, which we already do, and avoid browser-only tricks in the core.
  • Keep the mobile-first layout, and avoid features that only work on desktop.
  • Plan for HTTPS from the start, since phone cameras need it.
  • Make the upload flow work with the photo library, not only the camera, because that is the more reliable path on iOS.

Move to Capacitor if testers keep asking for it in the stores, or if iOS install friction or missing push notifications start costing you users. Move to React Native only if the web view's performance becomes a real complaint.

Turn 26

Lets not concern ourselves with apple suitability, just android also works
Claude's response

That simplifies things a lot. With Android only, I'd stay on the PWA and skip Capacitor and React Native entirely.

Why a PWA fits Android well

Chrome on Android is the best-supported platform for PWAs: - Install: Chrome shows an install prompt, and an installed PWA appears as a real app with its own icon, a splash screen and no browser bar. - Camera and gallery: the standard file input with capture works reliably, so the upload flow we built needs no changes. - Push notifications, background sync and storage: these are far more dependable than on iOS. - Updates: you deploy once and everyone has the new version, with no store review.

If you want to be in the Play Store

You don't need a wrapper. A Trusted Web Activity (TWA) packages your PWA as an Android app that opens it full-screen. Tools like Bubblewrap or PWABuilder generate it. From memory, it needs a Google Play developer account (a one-time fee of about $25, so check the current price), a verified link between your domain and the app, and a decent score on Chrome's PWA checks. It's mostly a packaging step, not new development.

What this changes in the plan

  • M8 is simpler. The manifest, service worker and install prompt only need to work in Android Chrome. I can drop the iOS Safari testing from the acceptance criteria.
  • Sign-in: the magic-link problem I flagged, where the Mail app opens Safari and not the installed app, mostly goes away on Android.
  • Not dropped: HTTPS is still required for the camera on a phone, and the web app must stay fast on mid-range Android phones. Lower-end devices struggle with the in-browser background removal, so keeping that optional (as it is now) is the right call.
  • Later: the Capacitor and React Native options only matter again if you want iOS.

I'll note this in DECISIONS.md so later milestones follow it.

Turn 27

why is having a local VLM a issue ?
Claude's response

A local VLM isn't a problem in itself. It's a good fit for development and private testing, and the trouble comes when other people use the app.

Where it works

On your own machine, with a GPU, the model runs next to npm run dev and your photos never leave your computer. Tagging costs nothing per photo.

Where it breaks

The app is meant to run on Vercel for real users, and several things then fail:

  • Vercel can't run it. Its serverless functions have no GPU, tight memory and time limits, and no place to keep a multi-gigabyte model loaded. The deployed app can't call a model that lives on your laptop. Your laptop isn't a public server, and it would have to be on and reachable all the time.
  • A GPU server costs money. To serve users you'd rent a GPU machine or a hosted inference service, usually billed by the hour whether or not anyone is using it. For a small beta that can cost more than the per-photo API price it was meant to save. I can't give you current prices.
  • Speed. A small model on modest hardware can take several seconds per photo, and concurrent users queue up. The spec's 20 photos in under 2 minutes target gets harder.
  • Quality is unproven. Smaller open models are usually weaker on fine details like jewellery types and exact colours. That is why the eval should decide, and why I wouldn't commit before measuring.
  • Maintenance. You'd own the model files, updates, GPU drivers and uptime, none of which an API makes you handle.

How to get the benefits anyway

  • Development and eval: use the local model freely. It saves API money while you iterate.
  • Production: keep a hosted API as the default, and treat the local or self-hosted model as an option behind the provider switch.
  • Later, if volume justifies it: deploy the model on a rented GPU or inference host. That only pays off at a scale you're unlikely to reach in the beta.

If you have a good GPU, a local model is a nice way to avoid API costs while building. It just can't be the thing real users depend on without more infrastructure.

  • The M8 work shrinks. There's no staging and production setup, and no public rate-limiting. Spend caps matter less when there's no API bill.
  • Remote access through SSH works with a port forward, for example ssh -L 3000:localhost:3000 you@this-machine. The remote person then opens localhost:3000 in their own browser. It's fine for a few trusted people.

Things that stay awkward

  • The phone. Your phone can't use an SSH tunnel by itself. It would need to reach the machine over the same Wi-Fi, or through a VPN-style tool such as Tailscale. The phone camera also needs HTTPS, and plain http://<LAN-IP> often blocks it. The Choose photos button still works.
  • Supabase is still in the cloud. That was your earlier choice. Photos and tags are stored there, and logins use its email links. Running everything locally would mean Docker and local Supabase, a separate decision.
  • Magic links: the redirect URLs must match however you reach the app (localhost, a LAN IP, a tunnel address).
  • The machine must be on. It's a single point of failure.

Can a CPU run the tagging model?

Probably yes, but I'd test before committing.

  • Speed: small vision-language models (a few billion parameters) can run on CPU. I'd expect several seconds to a minute per photo, depending on core count, RAM and the image size. The 20-photos-in-2-minutes target is realistic only with a fast CPU and a very small model, so that target may need loosening. I can't give you real numbers without knowing your hardware.
  • Quality is the bigger worry. Tagging looks simple, but it asks for a lot at once: a slot and a category from a fixed list, pattern, fabric, formality, season, neckline and metal tone, plus valid JSON. Models small enough for a CPU get fine distinctions wrong more often, especially jewellery types and regional garments like jhumkas versus drops.

A hybrid that helps a lot

Don't ask a small model to do everything:

  • Colours from the pixels, in code. Extract the dominant colours from the image directly (cutout plus clustering). That is more accurate than any VLM's guess at a hex value, and it's free.
  • Slot and category by classifier. A CLIP-style model can match the photo against your taxonomy labels. It's small, fast on CPU, and reliable for "is this a shoe, a necklace or a dress".
  • The VLM handles only the soft fields: formality, warmth, style tags, occasions, neckline.

Tell me your CPU model, core count and RAM, and whether there's any GPU. With that I can suggest a specific model size, and I'd benchmark one on your own photos before building the switch.

export type ImageInput = { mediaType: "image/jpeg" | "image/png"; base64: string };

export type Turn = { role: "user" | "model"; text: string; images?: ImageInput[] };

export type GenerateArgs = {
  apiKey: string;
  model: string;
  system: string;
  turns: Turn[];
  /** JSON Schema the output must satisfy. */
  jsonSchema: Record<string, unknown>;
  toolName: string;
  toolDescription: string;
  maxTokens: number;
  timeoutMs: number;
};

export type GenerateResult = { json: unknown; rawText: string; inputTokens: number; outputTokens: number };

export interface Provider {
  generate(args: GenerateArgs): Promise<GenerateResult>;
}

/** Transport-level failure (after provider-level retries). `status` is the HTTP status when known. */
export class ProviderError extends Error {
  constructor(
    message: string,
    public status?: number,
  ) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "ProviderError";
  }
}

export const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
export const isRetryable = (status?: number) => status === 429 || (status !== undefined && status >= 500);

import { isRetryable, ProviderError, sleep, type GenerateArgs, type GenerateResult, type Provider } from "./types";

const BASE = "https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta";
const MAX_RETRIES = 2;

type GeminiResponse = {
  candidates?: { content?: { parts?: { text?: string }[] }; finishReason?: string }[];
  usageMetadata?: { promptTokenCount?: number; candidatesTokenCount?: number; thoughtsTokenCount?: number };
  promptFeedback?: { blockReason?: string };
  error?: { message?: string };
};

/** Gemini's structured-output schema is a JSON Schema subset: strip keys it does not accept. */
export function toGeminiSchema(schema: unknown): unknown {
  if (Array.isArray(schema)) return schema.map(toGeminiSchema);
  if (schema && typeof schema === "object") {
    const out: Record<string, unknown> = {};
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(schema)) {
      if (k === "$schema" || k === "additionalProperties" || k === "propertyNames") continue;
      out[k] = toGeminiSchema(v);
    }
    return out;
  }
  return schema;
}

  async generate(args: GenerateArgs): Promise<GenerateResult> {
    const generationConfig: Record<string, unknown> = {

cat > tests/gemini.test.ts <<'EOF'
import { afterEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from "vitest";
import { geminiProvider, toGeminiSchema } from "@/lib/ai/providers/gemini";
import { ProviderError, type GenerateArgs } from "@/lib/ai/providers/types";

const args: GenerateArgs = {
  apiKey: "k",
  model: "gemini-2.5-flash",
  system: "sys",
  turns: [{ role: "user", text: "hi", images: [{ mediaType: "image/jpeg", base64: "AAAA" }] }],
  jsonSchema: { $schema: "x", type: "object", additionalProperties: false, properties: { a: { type: "string" } } },
  toolName: "t",
  toolDescription: "d",
  maxTokens: 100,
  timeoutMs: 1000,
};

const okBody = (text: string) => ({
  candidates: [{ content: { parts: [{ text }] } }],
  usageMetadata: { promptTokenCount: 10, candidatesTokenCount: 5, thoughtsTokenCount: 2 },
});
const res = (status: number, body: unknown) => new Response(JSON.stringify(body), { status });

afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks());

describe("toGeminiSchema", () => {
  it("strips keys Gemini rejects, recursively", () => {
    const out = toGeminiSchema({
      $schema: "x",
      type: "object",
      additionalProperties: false,
      properties: { a: { type: "object", additionalProperties: {}, properties: {} } },
    });
    expect(JSON.stringify(out)).not.toMatch(/additionalProperties|\$schema/);
  });
});

describe("geminiProvider", () => {
  it("sends image + schema and parses JSON, counting thinking tokens as output", async () => {
    const f = vi.spyOn(globalThis, "fetch").mockResolvedValue(res(200, okBody('{"a":"x"}')));
    const r = await geminiProvider.generate(args);
    expect(r.json).toEqual({ a: "x" });
    expect(r.inputTokens).toBe(10);
    expect(r.outputTokens).toBe(7);
    const [url, init] = f.mock.calls[0];
    expect(String(url)).toContain("gemini-2.5-flash:generateContent");
    expect((init!.headers as Record<string, string>)["x-goog-api-key"]).toBe("k");
    const body = JSON.parse(init!.body as string);
    expect(body.contents[0].parts[0].inline_data.data).toBe("AAAA");
    expect(body.generationConfig.responseMimeType).toBe("application/json");
    expect(body.generationConfig.thinkingConfig).toEqual({ thinkingBudget: 0 });
  });

  it("returns json=null (not a throw) when the text is not JSON, so the repair loop can run", async () => {
    vi.spyOn(globalThis, "fetch").mockResolvedValue(res(200, okBody("not json")));
    const r = await geminiProvider.generate(args);
    expect(r.json).toBeNull();
    expect(r.rawText).toBe("not json");
  });

  it("retries 429 then succeeds", async () => {
    const f = vi
      .spyOn(globalThis, "fetch")
      .mockResolvedValueOnce(res(429, { error: { message: "slow down" } }))
      .mockResolvedValueOnce(res(200, okBody("{}")));
    const r = await geminiProvider.generate(args);
    expect(r.json).toEqual({});
    expect(f).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  });

  it("does not retry a 400 and surfaces the status", async () => {
    const f = vi.spyOn(globalThis, "fetch").mockResolvedValue(res(400, { error: { message: "bad" } }));
    await expect(geminiProvider.generate(args)).rejects.toMatchObject({ status: 400 });
    expect(f).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  it("gives up after 3 attempts on persistent 500s", async () => {
    const f = vi.spyOn(globalThis, "fetch").mockResolvedValue(res(500, { error: { message: "boom" } }));
    await expect(geminiProvider.generate(args)).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(ProviderError);
    expect(f).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
  }, 10_000);

  it("reports blocked prompts", async () => {
    vi.spyOn(globalThis, "fetch").mockResolvedValue(res(200, { promptFeedback: { blockReason: "SAFETY" } }));
    await expect(geminiProvider.generate(args)).rejects.toThrow(/blocked/i);
  });
});

The tagger now runs on Gemini and works end to end against your real key. The AI client no longer depends on one vendor, and Anthropic is still available as a switch. Three live checks passed: a real photo from your closet was tagged and validated, a blank grey image was rejected as not clothing, and both calls were logged. 45 unit tests, typecheck and lint also pass.

Turn 32

Do we need to store pairwise compatibility ? is there no rule based way of determining this ?
Claude's response

Mostly no. The rule-based scores don't need storing. Only the results from the AI judge do.

What's already rule-based

pairScore() computes a pair's compatibility from colour harmony, formality, season, style and occasion overlap, the pattern rule, the metal rule and the neckline rule. It's pure code. Scoring every pair in a 100-item closet takes a few milliseconds, so storing those results saves nothing. We can recompute them whenever we need them, and they're always fresh because they're computed from the current tags. That also removes the stale-score problem for the rule layer.

Why store anything at all

Storing only pays off for outputs that are slow, costly or non-deterministic:

  • Vision-judge results: these cost an API call per batch, and re-asking can give a different answer. They should be saved once per pair and invalidated only when one of the items' tags changes. This is the only real use of pair_scores.
  • Curator and critic output (looks): also LLM output, so worth storing for the same reasons, and so anchor requests become fast lookups.
  • Your feedback: if you thumbs-down an outfit, that signal should persist and can override a score.

What I'd do

  1. Compute rule scores on demand, and don't store them.
  2. Keep pair_scores, but only for pairs the vision judge actually scored (source = 'vision'), plus any user override.
  3. Keep looks and wardrobe_graph_stats as designed.

This shrinks the table from thousands of rows per user to a few hundred at most. The schema doesn't change, so there's no new migration. I'd just stop writing source='rules' rows.

The other direction

You could also drop the vision judge entirely and use rules only. That is cheaper, fully deterministic, and has no API cost for pairs. The cost is quality. Rules can't see what a photo shows: whether two prints really clash, how a fabric drapes, whether a silhouette suits another, or whether a mid-scoring pair looks good together. The vision judge only touches the uncertain middle band, so the extra cost is bounded. I'd keep it, but it's the first thing to cut if you want to save API cost, and the eval can tell us how much it adds.

Do you want it as I described, with rules on demand and AI judgements stored? Or rules only for now, with the judge added later if the outfits feel mediocre?

Bash: cat > src/lib/ai/mock-tagger.ts <<'EOF' import { METAL_TONES, PATTERNS, SEASONS } from "@/lib/ai/tag
cat > src/lib/ai/mock-tagger.ts <<'EOF'
import { METAL_TONES, PATTERNS, SEASONS } from "@/lib/ai/tag-enums";
import { CATEGORIES_BY_SLOT, SLOTS, type Slot } from "@/lib/styling/taxonomy";
import type { TagResult } from "@/lib/ai/tagger";

/**
 * Offline stand-in for the real tagger (AI_PROVIDER=mock). Output is seeded from the image bytes, so the
 * same photo always gets the same tags. Used to exercise upload/review/rejection flows without API spend.
 */
export const MOCK_PROMPT_VERSION = "mock.v0";

/** FNV-1a over the base64 text (cheap, deterministic). */
export function imageSeed(base64: string): number {
  let h = 2166136261;
  for (let i = 0; i < base64.length; i += 7) h = Math.imul(h ^ base64.charCodeAt(i), 16777619);
  return h >>> 0;
}

function rng(seed: number) {
  let a = seed;
  return () => {
    a |= 0;
    a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}

/** About one photo in six is "not clothing", so the rejection flow gets exercised. */
export const mockRejects = (seed: number) => seed % 6 === 0;

export function mockTags(base64: string): TagResult {
  const seed = imageSeed(base64);
  const r = rng(seed);
  const pick = <T>(xs: readonly T[]): T => xs[Math.floor(r() * xs.length)];
  const int = (lo: number, hi: number) => lo + Math.floor(r() * (hi - lo + 1));
  const hex = () => `#${Math.floor(r() * 0xffffff).toString(16).padStart(6, "0")}`;
  const tag = seed.toString(16).slice(0, 4);

  const slot: Slot = pick(SLOTS);
  const category = pick(CATEGORIES_BY_SLOT[slot]) as TagResult["category"];
  const confidence = Object.fromEntries(
    ["slot", "category", "colors", "pattern", "fabric", "formality", "warmth", "seasons"].map((k) => [
      k,
      r() < 0.25 ? 0.3 + r() * 0.25 : 0.7 + r() * 0.3, // ~25% of fields come back low-confidence
    ]),
  );
  const wearsOnBody = slot === "top" || slot === "dress" || slot === "onepiece";

  return {
    is_wardrobe_item: !mockRejects(seed),
    rejection_reason: mockRejects(seed) ? `mock: photo ${tag} treated as not clothing` : undefined,
    slot,
    category,
    subcategory: `mock ${category.replace(/_/g, " ")} #${tag}`,
    colors: Array.from({ length: int(1, 3) }, (_, i) => ({
      name: `mock colour ${i + 1}`,
      hex: hex(),
      role: i === 0 ? ("primary" as const) : ("secondary" as const),
    })),
    pattern: pick(PATTERNS),
    fabric: pick(["cotton", "silk", "denim", "wool", "linen", "leather"]),
    formality: int(1, 5),
    warmth: int(1, 5),
    seasons: SEASONS.filter(() => r() < 0.5),
    neckline: wearsOnBody ? pick(["v-neck", "crew neck", "scoop", "off-shoulder", "high neck"]) : undefined,
    statement_level: int(1, 5),
    metal_tone: slot.startsWith("jewellery") ? pick(METAL_TONES) : undefined,
    style_tags: [pick(["minimal", "boho", "classic", "street", "festive"])],
    occasions: [pick(["casual", "work", "party", "wedding", "travel"])],
    confidence,
  };
}
