Conclusion: raw hex digits are a poor input (a digit's size says nothing about the colour: #a8 and #a9 are the same colour, #0f and #10 are far apart), and depth hurts with this much data (10 layers worse than 2 on the same Lab input, and far worse than the shipped design). The shipped design already beats the rater's own test-retest (Spearman 0.44 on 49 repeats). Smoothing the rater's drift is a data and loss question (more raters, one rater offset and scale per person, more rated pairs), not a depth question.

## Rater-aware colour training; model retrained on 685 pairs (2026-10-24)
- **Why:** a second rater is joining, and the owner's own repeats agree only 76% within 1 point (MAE 0.86), so consistency is the colour model's weak spot. Pooling raters naively would mix scales.
- **How** (`experiments/colour-pairs/raters.py`): each rater r is `rating = a_r + b_r * y(pair) + noise_r`. y is the shared network on the reference rater's scale (the rater with most ratings, a = 0, b = 1). Training alternates: fit the network on every rater's ratings mapped to the reference scale, weighted by 1 / (repeat noise + 0.05); then refit a_r, b_r, shrunk toward (0, 1) with a prior of 20 ratings. With one rater it is the plain training. The rater scales and weights are stored in `model.json` (the closet ignores them). Cross-validation folds by pair, so all raters' ratings of one pair stay together, and each rater is checked on their own scale.
- **Test:** a simulated harsh, narrow, noisier second rater: the scale is recovered (offset -0.5, stretch 0.6) and pooling does not hurt.
- **Retrained** on 685 pairs (734 ratings, 1 rater): unseen pairs 0.65, unseen colours 0.61. Shipped to `src/lib/styling/colour-pair-model.json`; golden fixture regenerated.
- **Fingerprint:** `COLOUR_MODEL_ID` (the model's ratings on 4 fixed pairs) is now in the item fingerprint, so a retrained model re-scores stored pairs; before, only a config change did.
- **Retrained (same day) on 1020 pairs** (1109 ratings, all samples rated): owner's repeats now 85% within 1 point (MAE 0.62, was 76% / 0.86); unseen pairs 0.69, unseen colours 0.64 (were 0.65 / 0.61). Shipped; golden fixture regenerated.

## Garment -> silhouette pool: product-only shop photos joined to the old pool (2026-10-24)
- **Why:** a third of the first pool's cut-outs (photos of models, cut by the u2net clothing segmenter) were torn, and the pool was Princess Polly only, so it was skewed toward camis, halters, wide-leg pants and minis.
- **How** (`experiments/silhouette-match/web_pool.py`): public Shopify feeds (`/products.json`; robots.txt checked, 1 feed request/s, honest user agent). Per top or bottom, CLIP (ViT-B-32) picks the product's photo most likely to be the garment alone (flat-lay / ghost mannequin, p >= 0.6). The background is a smooth surface fitted to the photo border and flood-filled away, so no segmentation model and no tearing. The same completeness check as the pool, "accept" only; near-copies of an outline already kept from the shop (same cut, other colour) are skipped. Dresses, outerwear, knitwear (incl. turtlenecks / mock necks), sets, swim and underwear are skipped (no library drawings). Each style bucket (`KINDS`, e.g. jeans, cami, corset) is capped at 45 in the joined pool, so the denim shops could not keep adding jeans.
- **Joined pool** (`skew.py`): the old pool's clean cut-outs (178; labels marked bad or none-fit are left out) + 556 shop garments = 734; 60% tops; 76% product-only. Largest top style tee 15%, largest bottom style jeans 26%; largest shop Princess Polly 24%. 19 shop garments are marked `excluded` (kept on disk, not used).
- **Not automated:** torn pale fabric and the odd model photo that passes CLIP. Neither a hole count, a morphological-closing measure nor a skin check separated them (skin fires on beige garments, closing on the gap between trouser legs); they are caught by eye during labelling and marked bad. `train.py --labels` now skips labels marked bad.

Got the first report back: the existing ItemEditor (in review/carousel.tsx) is reusable as a standalone tag editor for the detail page, with a small gap — it's missing fit, length, pattern_detail, garment_detail fields that exist in the schema but were never wired into the UI. Still waiting on the segmentation/colour-extraction pipeline investigation before I plan the second half.

Both investigations are in. Reusing the existing ItemEditor for a "review tags" entry on the detail page is straightforward — I'll build that now. "use client";

import { useRouter } from "next/navigation";
import { useState } from "react";
import { Pencil, X } from "lucide-react";
import { ItemEditor, type ReviewItem } from "@/app/(app)/closet/review/carousel";

/** Lets a user open the same tag editor used in review, see the current tags for an
 * already-confirmed item, and change or delete it. */
export function TagReviewModal({ item }: { item: ReviewItem }) {
  const router = useRouter();
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <>
      <button
        onClick={() => setOpen(true)}
        className="muted inline-flex items-center gap-1 text-sm underline underline-offset-4"
      >
        <Pencil size={14} aria-hidden="true" />
        Review tags
      </button>
      {open && (
        <div
          role="dialog"
          aria-modal="true"
          aria-label="Review tags"
          className="fixed inset-0 z-50 overflow-y-auto bg-black/70 p-4"
        >
          <div className="mx-auto max-w-md rounded-xl border border-[var(--line)] bg-[var(--bg)] p-4">
            <div className="mb-3 flex items-center justify-between">
              <h2 className="text-lg font-semibold">Review tags</h2>
              <button onClick={() => setOpen(false)} aria-label="Close">
                <X size={18} aria-hidden="true" />
              </button>
            </div>
            <ItemEditor
              item={item}
              onSaved={() => {
                setOpen(false);
                router.refresh();
              }}
              onDeleted={() => {
                setOpen(false);
                router.push("/closet");
              }}
            />
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </>
  );
}

## "Review tags" on the item detail page reuses the review carousel's editor (2026-10-25)

No changes to `ItemEditor` itself, so behavior matches the existing review flow exactly, including its own built-in Delete button.
- **Known gap carried over, not fixed here:** `ItemEditor` doesn't render `fit`, `length`, `pattern_detail`, or `garment_detail`, even though `EditableTags` (`src/lib/schemas.ts`) supports them — this gap already existed in the untagged-review flow and wasn't introduced by this change. Left as-is to avoid scope creep; worth a follow-up if those fields need to be user-editable.
EOF

# Clothes Segmentation using U2NET #

![Python 3.8](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.8-green.svg)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-green.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1EhEy3uQh-5oOSagUotVOJAf8m7Vqn0D6?usp=sharing)

This repo contains training code, inference code and pre-trained model for Cloths Parsing from human portrait.</br>
Here clothes are parsed into 3 category: Upper body(red), Lower body(green) and Full body(yellow)

![Sample 000](assets/000.png)
![Sample 024](assets/024.png)
![Sample 018](assets/018.png)

This model works well with any background and almost all poses. For more samples visit [samples.md](samples.md)

# Techinal details

* **U2NET** : This project uses an amazing [U2NET](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.09007) as a deep learning model. Instead of having 1 channel output from u2net for typical salient object detection task it outputs 4 channels each respresting upper body cloth, lower body cloth, fully body cloth and background. Only categorical cross-entropy loss is used for a given version of the checkpoint.

* **Dataset** : U2net is trained on 45k images [iMaterialist (Fashion) 2019 at FGVC6](https://www.kaggle.com/c/imaterialist-fashion-2019-FGVC6/data) dataset. To reduce complexity, I have clubbed the original 42 categories from dataset labels into 3 categories (upper body, lower body and full body). All images are resized into square `¯\_(ツ)_/¯` 768 x 768 px for training. (This experiment was conducted with 768 px but around 384 px will work fine too if one is retraining on another dataset).

# Training 

- For training this project requires,
<ul>
    <ul>
    <li>&nbsp; PyTorch > 1.3.0</li>
    <li>&nbsp; tensorboardX</li>
    <li>&nbsp; gdown</li>
    </ul>
</ul>

- Download dataset from this [link](https://www.kaggle.com/c/imaterialist-fashion-2019-FGVC6/data), extract all items.
- Set path of `train` folder which contains training images and `train.csv` which is label csv file in `options/base_options.py`
- To port original u2net of all layer except last layer please run `python setup_model_weights.py` and it will generate weights after model surgey in `prev_checkpoints` folder.
- You can explore various options in `options/base_options.py` like checkpoint saving folder, logs folder etc.
- For single gpu set `distributed = False` in `options/base_options.py`, for multi gpu set it to `True`.
- For single gpu run `python train.py`
- For multi gpu run <br>
&nbsp;`python -m torch.distributed.launch --nnodes=1 --node_rank=0 --nproc_per_node=4 --use_env train.py` <br>
Here command is for single node, 4 gpu. Tested only for single node.
- You can watch loss graphs and samples in tensorboard by running tensorboard command in log folder.


# Testing/Inference
- Download pretrained model from this [link](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mhF3yqd7R-Uje092eypktNl-RoZNuiCJ/view?usp=sharing)(165 MB) in `trained_checkpoint` folder.
- Put input images in `input_images` folder
- Run `python infer.py` for inference.
- Output will be saved in `output_images`
### OR 
- Inference in colab from here [![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1EhEy3uQh-5oOSagUotVOJAf8m7Vqn0D6?usp=sharing)

# Acknowledgements
- U2net model is from original [u2net repo](https://github.com/xuebinqin/U-2-Net). Thanks to Xuebin Qin for amazing repo.
- Complete repo follows structure of [Pix2pixHD repo](https://github.com/NVIDIA/pix2pixHD)

Vercel's documented limit for standard Serverless Functions is 250 MB unzipped, but the newest guidance I found also mentions an opt-in path for larger functions.

- **Standard limit:** Vercel's troubleshooting guide, last updated May 2026, says the maximum uncompressed size is 250 MB (approximately 50 MB compressed). It adds that this limit is not configurable.
- **Newer guide (July 2026):** A later version of the same guide says the standard limit is 250 MB, or about 500 MB uncompressed for Python, and describes opting into large Functions or reducing the bundle. This conflicts with the May version's claim that the limit cannot be changed, so the current docs should be checked directly.
- **Python 500 MB claim:** A Vercel community reply says Python's limit doubled to 500MB unzipped (previously 250MB). I did not find the official changelog it cites, so treat that figure as unconfirmed.
- **Diagnosing size:** The guide suggests setting VERCEL_ANALYZE_BUILD_OUTPUT=1 so build logs show uncompressed function sizes and the largest contributors.
- **Common causes:** Large heavy libraries or many packages get bundled, and unneeded files such as source maps, documentation, tests, build artifacts, or caches can also end up in the bundle.

     1 +/** The local calendar date (YYYY-MM-DD) of a moment, in the ru

     2 +export function localDate(d: Date = new Date()): string {      
     3 +  const p = (n: number) => String(n).padStart(2, "0");         
     4 +  return `${d.getFullYear()}-${p(d.getMonth() + 1)}-${p(d.getDa
       +te())}`;                                                       
     5 +}                                                              
     6 +                                                               
     7 +/** The last `n` local dates ending today, oldest first. */    
     8 +export function lastDays(n: number, today: Date = new Date()): 
       +string[] {                                                     
     9 +  return Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => {                 
    10 +    const d = new Date(today);                                 
    11 +    d.setDate(d.getDate() - (n - 1 - i));                      
    12 +    return localDate(d);                                       
    13 +  });                                                          
    14 +}

The UI milestone is committed (7fb4710). While the background agent finishes its cut-out experiments, I'll read the upload chain myself so I can judge its findings rather than take them on trust:
Searched for 1 pattern, ran 1 shell command
Here's where things stand: the UI work is done, the cut-out research is still running in the background, and phase 2 isn't finished yet. UI (committed as 7fb4710) - Themes: four of them. Atelier, a warm ivory/ink/terracotta light theme, is the new default. Noir is the previous dark look with lit light boxes, plus Rosé and Sage. You switch on the new "You" page, and the choice is remembered. - Default changed from dark to light: you'd earlier asked for a dark wardrobe, but black and navy garments vanished on it. Noir is one tap away if you prefer it. - New screens: - Today: an outfit of the day picked for the weather, your week, unworn pieces you could "rediscover", and stats. - Mix & match: swipe tops and bottoms and see the match score update live, with shuffle, lock and "best partner". - Saved looks and "Wore it" buttons, with a wear diary. - You: your colour palette, outfits per occasion with the missing piece named, and the theme picker. - Redesigned screens: - Closet: a colour filter and a rails/grid toggle. - Item page: colours, formality and warmth meters, "Mix with this", "Wore it". - Add and review: tap scales and chips instead of number boxes. - Desktop: a sidebar layout instead of a narrow phone column. - Weather: your OpenWeather key in .env.local is blank, so I used Open-Meteo, which needs no key. - Checks: typecheck, lint (no errors) and the production build pass. All 280 tests pass on their own runs. One existing test, in detections.test.ts, timed out in the full-suite run while the background agent was loading the machine; it passes alone, and I'll re-run the full suite when it's done. I also clicked through save → Saved page → "Wore it" → diary in a real browser, then removed the test rows from the demo account. Pipeline: one confirmed bug so far Several cut-outs in your closet are completely transparent. The background remover erased the whole garment and the app stored the empty result without checking. That's why the navy top, the black tank and the floral dress show as blank cards. The new light theme makes this visible; the dark theme hid it. How the chain works: 1. A Gemini call finds a box around each garment. 2. That region is cropped out of the full-size photo. 3. A general background remover (@imgly) runs on the crop. It doesn't know about clothing, so it keeps skin and bodies, and it can erase garments that are close in colour to the background. 4. Colours and the silhouette match are both measured from that cut-out, so a bad cut-out corrupts both. The tagger sees the original crop, so it isn't affected. The background agent is now testing other cut-out methods against hand-checked masks: a clothing-specific segmenter, box-prompted SAM-style models, and a human-parsing model to strip skin and hair. It's also looking at a quality gate for empty cut-outs and at why some crops are tiny (143×96 px). When it reports back, I'll check its evidence, wire the winning method into the app, and re-run the pipeline end to end.

       + maxSoftRatio: 0.35 } as const;

     9 +export function cutoutGate(rgba: ArrayLike<number>): { ok: bool
       +ean; opaque: number; soft: number } {                          
    10 +  const n = Math.floor(rgba.length / 4);                       
    11 +  if (!n) return { ok: false, opaque: 0, soft: 0 };            
    12 +  let solid = 0;                                               
    13 +  let soft = 0;                                                
    14 +  for (let i = 3; i < rgba.length; i += 4) {

    16 +    if (a >= 0.5) solid++;                                     
    17 +    if (a > 0.1 && a < 0.9) soft++;                            
    18 +  }                                                            
    19 +  const opaque = solid / n;                                    
    20 +  const softShare = soft / n;                                  
    21 +  const ok =                                                   
    22 +    opaque >= CUTOUT_GATE.minOpaque &&                         
    23 +    opaque <= CUTOUT_GATE.maxOpaque &&                         
    24 +    softShare / Math.max(opaque + softShare, 1e-6) <= CUTOUT_GA
       +TE.maxSoftRatio;                                               
    25 +  return { ok, opaque, soft: softShare };

The backfill re-cut all 24 items, but some silhouette picks are off (e.g., khaki trousers tagged "classic shorts") — a pre-existing matcher weakness, not a masking issue, which I'll flag as a next step. Now I'll trigger pair re-scoring so matches use the corrected colors, then check the closet.
Read 1 file, ran 1 shell command
All garments are now visible, with a few minor leftover flaws (skin patches, the kept belt, a small trouser nick) and one untagged blurry item that'll be re-cut once tagged. Now I'll run the full end-to-end test by uploading the coat/shirt/trousers photo through the Add flow while the server re-cut runs in the background.

Tracing the full chain, I found the main issue: the tagger mislabeled the "Black Coat" box as checked trousers since its crop is mostly trousers, creating a duplicate and losing the coat. The cheap fix is to pass the detector's original "Black Coat" label as a hint instead of discarding it—checking the tagger and its prompt now.

Both parts are done, tested and committed: the UI redesign (7fb4710) and the pipeline fix (82df120). The cut-out was the main thing hurting results, and it's fixed with measured evidence. A few weaker stages further down the chain are still open; they're listed at the end. 1. UI redesign - Four themes: Atelier (warm ivory, ink and terracotta) is the new default. Noir is your earlier dark look with lit light boxes, plus Rosé and Sage. You switch on the new "You" page and the choice is remembered. - Default changed from dark to light: you'd asked for a dark wardrobe, but black and navy clothes vanished on it. Noir is one tap away if you prefer it. - New screens: - Today: an outfit of the day that suits the weather and skips anything you wore in the last few days. Plus your week, unworn pieces to "rediscover", and stats. - Mix & match: swipe tops and bottoms and see the match score live, with shuffle, lock and "best partner". - Saved looks and "Wore it", with a wear diary. - You: your colour palette, outfits per occasion (it names the missing piece, e.g. "add a bottom for formal"), and the theme picker. - Redesigned: - Closet: a colour filter and a rails/grid toggle. - Item page: colours, formality and warmth, "Mix with this". - Add flow: drag-and-drop. - Review screen: tap scales and chips instead of number boxes. - Desktop: a sidebar layout instead of a narrow phone column. - Inspiration: Whering's outfit shuffle, Acloset and Alta's weather-based daily outfit, Indyx's wardrobe stats. - Weather: your OpenWeather key in .env.local is blank, so I used Open-Meteo, which needs no key. 2. Pipeline: what was wrong and what I changed - The cut-out (mask) was broken: 13 of your 23 garment cut-outs were completely transparent or see-through, and the app saved them without checking. That's why several garments showed as blank cards. - Testing: a background agent compared 7 methods against 24 masks it drew and checked by eye. A clothing-parser model scored 0.90 overlap with the true mask versus 0.56 for the old method. Colour accuracy measured from the cut-outs went from 0.47 to 0.89. - New server cut-out: the server now re-cuts every newly tagged item with the clothing parser. It saves the result next to the old file instead of overwriting it, re-measures colours, and re-runs the silhouette match. It's a local Python step like your silhouette matcher, so a serverless deploy won't have it. - Safer browser cut-out: for that case it pads the image before cutting (overlap 0.56 → 0.75) and rejects empty or see-through results instead of storing them. - Existing items: I re-cut all 24 demo items and re-scored pairs. Every garment now shows. I saved a backup of the old values first, in a git-ignored file. - Tagger fix from a real photo test: I uploaded a coat/shirt/check-trousers photo through the app. The open coat got tagged as the trousers underneath it. The garment detector had already labelled that box "Black Coat", so the tagger now receives that label as a hint (tagger.v13). Correct slots went from 13/15 to 15/15 on your hand-labelled crops, with no regressions. - Cleanup: deleting an item now removes all its files, including old cut-outs. The test uploads, saved looks and wear entries are removed, so the demo account is back to its earlier contents, apart from the re-cut items and re-scored pairs above. Checks: typecheck, lint and the production build pass, and all 288 tests pass. Still weak, in order 1. Colour names: a black coat comes out "charcoal", a white shirt "pale grey", brown/cream gingham "charcoal". This feeds pair scoring directly. Fixing it properly needs a small hand-labelled colour set, which doesn't exist yet. 2. Silhouette matcher: low confidence and some wrong picks (khaki trousers → "classic shorts"), even with clean cut-outs. 3. Intermittent "Not signed in" on upload: it happened in 1 of 3 test runs and didn't come back on retry. I haven't found the cause. Colour naming is the next thing I'd tackle. All of this is recorded in STATUS.md and DECISIONS.md. Sources: - The Best Wardrobe Apps 2026 (Indyx) - Indyx vs Whering 2026 (StylePal) - Best Wardrobe Apps 2026 (Wardrowbe) - Best AI Wardrobe Apps 2026 (aurelle)

The TypeScript picker differs from the Python original in minimum share and lighting rules. I'll fix it directly in production code, starting by building the image set.

All 24 line up. Baseline run:
Ran 1 shell command
Baseline accuracy is 54% (20/37) overall and 0/3 on two-colour fabrics, with misses mostly from lighting darkening/dulling colours (whites→pale_grey, black→charcoal, etc.) and patterns being averaged into one colour. I'll check the odd jeans→61% black result before experimenting further.
Read 1 file, ran 1 shell command
Only 17% of the jeans' pixels are dark, yet the picker reports 61% black. Something in the pipeline is off, so I'll trace it:
Ran 1 shell command
Pixel extraction checks out (18% dark), so the bug must be in the picker's clustering/merging logic. I'll build an instrumented, parameterized copy of the picker that prints each intermediate step for testing variants.

Found the bug: the "transition colours" step meant to remove blurry boundaries was wrongly classifying smooth gradients (like shaded denim) as transitions, deleting two-thirds of the jeans' color clusters and leaving only shadow and highlight. I'm now checking whether this same issue explains the other misses.
Ran 1 shell command
Three issues explain most misses: averaging washes out lit vs. shadow tones, paint-chip names don't match camera-recorded black/white ranges, and low-res resizing blurs fine patterns like gingham. I'll test fixes one at a time—naming by lit-tone percentile, calibrating swatches to camera range, tightening the edge-detection rule, and raising sampling resolution—starting by making resize resolution a backward-compatible parameter.

Running a grid search across 576 settings for the 37 garments, using leave-one-out so each garment is scored on settings tuned from the other 36 to avoid overfitting the test set.
Ran 1 shell command
The search is bigger than I estimated (1,200 combinations) and is still running in the background. While it runs, one consideration about the calibration idea. It risks overcorrecting real mid-tones, for example turning a genuine charcoal garment into black. The labelled set has no true charcoal or light-grey garment except the grey ribbed trousers. So whatever wins, I'll also check it against the existing picker unit tests, which include greys and stripes, before porting.

Combining all four fixes raises accuracy to 32/37 primary and 1/3 two-colour, with patterns remaining the main weakness. Let me look at what's still being missed.
Ran 1 shell command
The remaining misses split into borderline color calls, a badly underexposed photo, and gingham patterns losing their light squares — that last one's a clear bug, so I'll trace it next.
Ran 1 shell command
Found it: the lighting step merges light clusters into the main color as highlights, but on patterned garments that wrongly swallows gingham/print whites. The fix is to check the garment's pattern field (already determined before color measurement) and preserve distinct light clusters as a second color when patterned—so next I'll pull the pattern info for each test garment.

Claude's response
The dev server is still running. Checking it responds:
Searched for 1 pattern, ran 1 shell command
Yes, it's running now: - On this Mac: http://localhost:3000 - On your phone (same Wi-Fi): http://10.192.241.41:3000. The layout is built for phone screens. - Sign in: use "Open the demo" on the login page; the password (fashion2rock) is pre-filled. What you'll see: - Live now: the redesigned UI and the fixed cut-outs. All 24 demo garments were re-cut, so none are blank any more. - Not live yet: the colour fix is still experimental. Colour names in the app are the old ones, so a black coat still says "charcoal". I'm finishing that now. - Adding photos works end to end, but the server cut-out step runs on this Mac, so keep it awake. Packaging it as a deployable app (Docker) The reason Docker is needed: two pipeline steps, the silhouette matcher and the new cut-out, are Python models that the Next.js server calls directly. That rules out Vercel-style serverless hosting. You need a long-running container on a VM or a container host. The database, login and file storage are already on hosted Supabase, so they move as they are. Step: Docker image What's involved: Node + Python in one image, CPU-only PyTorch, model weights (~650 MB) downloaded at build time so the first request isn't slow. Image ≈ 3 GB. Effort: ~½ day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Keep models loaded What's involved: Right now each cut-out reloads its model (~8 s per garment). A small always-on Python worker cuts that to ~1 s. Not required, but strongly recommended. Effort: ~½ day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Host + domain What's involved: A machine with ≥ 4 GB RAM (a small VPS from Hetzner or DigitalOcean, or Fly.io / Railway / Render, roughly $10–30/month), HTTPS, environment secrets, and adding the new domain to Supabase's allowed login URLs. Effort: ~½ day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Must-fix before strangers use it What's involved: The intermittent "Not signed in" upload error, a health check, error logging. Effort: ~½–1 day ──────────────────────────────────────── Step: Spec's full launch list (M8) What's involved: Rate limits, Sentry, installable phone app, privacy pages, staging + production copies. Effort: +2–3 days My estimate: about 1.5–2 days to a working deployed app you can share, and 4–5 days to the spec's full production standard. Mostly that's careful setup rather than new features. One decision would change the plan. If you'd rather avoid running a server, the Python steps can be dropped in production. The app already falls back to the browser cut-out, which is now padded and quality-gated, and to the simpler silhouette rules. Then it could deploy to Vercel in a few hours, at the cost of lower-quality cut-outs (0.75 overlap vs 0.90). I'll finish the colour work first. It's waiting on one validation run. After that, let me know whether you want the Docker deployment and where you'd like to host it.

Ran 1 shell command
The colour fix is done, committed (3e3ac8d), and live on http://localhost:3000. The demo closet's colours have been re-measured. Results I had no ground truth, so I built a labelled set first: 39 garments, with the acceptable colour names marked by eye. Two were excluded because their masks are wrong, leaving 37 scored.
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬───────┐ │ │ Before │ After │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Main colour right │ 20/37 │ 32/37 │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Two-colour fabrics (gingham, block print): both colours │ 0/3 │ 3/3 │ │ found │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────┘
To guard against tuning to the test set, I tuned on half the garments and scored on the other half, both ways round: 10/13 vs 4/13 for the old picker, and 22/24 vs 14/24. Both halves independently chose the same settings, and those are what shipped. Honest caveat: on brand-new photos expect somewhat less than 32/37. What was wrong, and the fixes 1. A real bug: the picker deleted most of some garments. A step meant to drop the blurry edge between two colours also removed the middle of any fabric under natural shading. The jeans lost two-thirds of their pixels and came out "61% black". 2. Colours were named by their average, shadows included. A cream satin skirt averaged out to "taupe". The picker now names each colour by its well-lit part. 3. The reference colours were paint chips. Cameras rarely record pure white, so white tops came out "pale grey". Names are now matched against the colour list as a camera records it. 4. Light pattern colours were treated as highlights. The gingham's white squares disappeared into the blue. When the tagger says a garment is patterned, a clearly lighter colour is now kept as part of the pattern. What you'll see in the app - White tops now say white instead of pale grey, and the cream skirt says beige instead of taupe. - The light-blue top is now powder blue + white, the gingham light wash + white, and the floral set gets its pinks + white. - Pairs are being re-scored in the background with the new colours. - The 4 items whose tags you had already confirmed were left untouched. The old colours are backed up in a git-ignored file. Still wrong - Black wool coat → "charcoal". The other three black garments are right. - A badly underexposed rust dress → "oxblood". - Jeans read as plain grey. That's true to those pixels, but you'd call it "mid wash". All of this is recorded in DECISIONS.md and STATUS.md. Typecheck, lint, all 291 tests and the production build pass. Ready for the Docker deployment whenever you are. Tell me which host you want; my default is Fly.io. I'll build and test the container here first, and you'll only need to do the account login step.

Turn 182

If we use a docker and all will I get a link I can share with other people ?
Claude's response
Yes. Strictly, Docker only packages the app; the shareable link comes from running that package on a hosting service. With Fly.io you'd get a permanent HTTPS address like https://closet-aina.fly.dev, and anyone can open it on their phone or laptop. You can put it on your own domain later if you want. What happens when someone opens the link - They sign in with their email and get a magic link, or tap the demo button. - Everyone who uses their own email gets a private closet. - Everyone who uses the demo button shares one closet, so they'd see and change each other's clothes. That's fine for a quick look, less so for real use. Three things to fix before sharing widely 1. Sign-in emails. Supabase's built-in email sender only allows a few emails per hour, so if several people sign up at once, some won't get their link. The fix is to connect a free email service such as Resend (~15 minutes; you'd create the account). 2. AI costs. Every upload calls Gemini to detect, tag and pair garments. You already have a daily spend cap and a demo-account limit configured, so costs can't run away, but busy days may hit the cap and pause tagging. 3. The intermittent "Not signed in" upload error I saw once. I should fix that before strangers see it. If you want to show someone today, before any of that: I can open a temporary public link straight to this Mac using a tunnel (Cloudflare or ngrok). That takes about 5 minutes, but it only works while your Mac is on and awake, and it's slower. It's fine for showing a few friends tonight, not as a permanent link. Since that puts your local app on the public internet, I'll only do it if you say so. So the options are: - Temporary link now (tunnel, about 5 minutes, needs your Mac on), or - Permanent link (Docker + Fly.io, same day: about 3–5 hours of my work, plus a few minutes of you creating the Fly account and logging in). Which do you want? Or both: the tunnel now, then the permanent deploy.

       +eaders }): string {                                            
     8 +  const fallback = new URL(request.url);                       
     9 +  const host = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-host")?.split("
       +,")[0].trim();                                                 
    10 +  if (!host || !/^[a-z0-9.-]+(:\d{1,5})?$/i.test(host)) return 
       +fallback.origin;                                               
    11 +  const proto = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-proto")?.split
       +(",")[0].trim();                                               
    12 +  const scheme = proto === "http" || proto === "https" ? proto 
       +: fallback.protocol.replace(":", "");                          
    13 +  return `${scheme}://${host}`;

Notably, the attribute bridge (which ignores the image entirely) crushes the shipped trained matcher (0.63 vs 0.19 top-1), and with the gate it hits 0.66/0.88 with zero family errors — meaning the live matcher was actually hurting results. Since it draws on different evidence, I'll export its scores and test fusing it with image + text.

Fusing in the bridge gives mixed results (top-1 and MRR improve, but top-5 slips slightly), and on only 32 garments that's not a clear win—so I'll ship image + text + family gate, keeping the gated bridge as fallback. Next, I'll check whether this holds up separately on the demo closet and test-set photo halves.

That doesn't help. Even at the 30th percentile the black coat reads lightness ~14, which still sits nearer charcoal than black once the camera range is applied, and one other garment got worse. The camera genuinely recorded that wool as very dark grey, and telling black from charcoal would need an exposure reference in the photo. I'll record it as a negative result and leave the shipped picker alone. Here's where the model-quality work stands. The cut-out agent is still running. Done and committed (ac32e99) 1. Silhouette matching: replaced. This was the biggest gain. The old matcher had only ever been tested on its own training photos. On the app's real cut-outs it put 10 of 18 trousers in the skirt or shorts family, and it was worse than the simple fallback it replaced. The new matcher compares the garment's image with both the silhouette drawings and their names, and only considers the family the tagger's category allows.
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬───────┐ │ On 32 labelled garments from your closet │ Before │ After │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Right silhouette ranked first │ 0.19 │ 0.72 │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Right silhouette in the top 5 │ 0.50 │ 0.94 │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤ │ Trousers matched as skirts or shorts │ 10/18 │ 0/18 │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────┘
- Honesty checks: the gain holds on both halves of the set. I also checked the new picks against the actual drawings by eye, because my labels partly use names and so does the new method; the visual check confirms them. - Confidence now means something: it was 0.1–0.4 before. Now, when it says ~0.7, it's right about 70% of the time. - Your closet is updated: khaki trousers are now matched as dhoti pants (was classic shorts), and the palazzo as palazzo pants (was paper-bag shorts). 2. Ranking bug fixed. "Ranking is not a permutation" made the app throw away good AI rankings; it happened 12 times in one log. Malformed answers are now repaired, and good passes are kept. 3. Colour: the black-coat fix didn't work (above), so nothing changed there. Still running: the cut-out agent, on skin patches, the white top worn on skin, the belt kept on the shirt, and rough edges on small crops. For you, tomorrow: press "Re-score all pairs" (Style page) once the demo AI budget resets. It's the only step that brings the new silhouette matches into the match scores. I held off today because, with no budget left, a re-score would replace your AI-ranked scores with rule-only ones. Can't be measured here: overall outfit match quality. Your rated outfits live in a labeler/data/ folder that isn't on this Mac. If you can copy it over, I can measure and tune matching against your own ratings.

The UI is far better, 1. why is the user asked to box the garments themselves? why not use the segmenter? the segmenter was working alright I belive? also in the mix and match I can see that many pairs have been left unscored why is that the case ?
Claude's response
Good questions. I'll check the facts before answering both.
Ran 1 shell command
Both have clear causes, and neither is the segmenter misbehaving. 1. Why you were asked to draw boxes Normally you aren't. Every photo first goes to an AI garment finder that boxes each garment automatically; you only untick what you don't want. In my earlier end-to-end test it found all 5 pieces (coat, shirt, trousers, bag, shoes) in about 6 seconds. What you hit today is the daily AI budget. The finder is a Gemini call, and the demo account's token budget is used up (the server log shows POST /api/items/detect 429). When the finder fails, the app falls back to "drag a box round each garment". That fallback is what you saw. You're right that the local clothes parser I use for cut-outs could do this job. It runs on this machine and costs nothing, and it already labels every pixel as top, trousers, skirt, dress, bag, shoes and so on. Boxes around those regions would make garment-finding work even with no AI budget, offline, or when Gemini is rate-limited. The AI finder is still probably better for flat-lays of several separate garments and for accessories. So my suggestion: use the parser as the automatic fallback (measured against the 9 hand-boxed test photos), and consider making it the primary finder if it scores close. 2. Why many Mix & match pairs are unscored Your closet has 11 tops × 11 bottoms = 121 possible pairs: - 83 are scored. Those are exactly the pairs that share an occasion (casual with casual, work with work…). - 38 are unscored. The app has a rule that two items are only scored together if they share an occasion, so a festive top is never paired with gym shorts. In Mix & match you're choosing pairs yourself, so that rule just leaves gaps. - Of the 83, only 16 have an AI-ranked score. The other 67 use the rule-based score, because the AI ranker ran out of budget, the same cause as #1. The fix: compute the rule-based score for every pair on the spot in Mix & match. It's local, instant and free. Cross-occasion pairs would show a note like "different occasions: work top with festive skirt". The AI ranker stays limited to sensible pairs to save budget. And tomorrow's "Re-score all pairs" will turn more of the 67 rule scores into AI-ranked ones. ⏺ User answered Claude's questions: ⎿  · Should I build these two fixes now? → As long as the segmenter is the gemini one when credits are there that is good enough. in that case ther is nothing to change right I believe ?
Right, nothing to change there. When there are credits, every photo goes to the Gemini garment finder and the boxes appear automatically. You only saw the manual boxes today because the budget had run out, and that resets tomorrow. Even then nothing breaks: you can draw boxes or add the whole photo. One thing worth knowing: the demo account shares a single daily budget among everyone who uses it, so if several people try the shared link on the same day, they can run it out again. If that happens, raising DEMO_DAILY_TOKENS in .env.local fixes it, at the cost of more Gemini spend. On the hosted version you'd change it in the Space's settings instead. I haven't changed Mix & match. The 38 unscored pairs are cross-occasion combinations, so they'll stay unscored until you want that changed. Instant rule-based scores for every pair would take me about 30 minutes whenever you want it.

     3 +/**                                                            
     4 + * The browser side of bring-your-own-key (src/lib/ai/byok.ts):

       +ite works without one (on the owner's key and limits).         
     7 + */                                                            
     8 +const STORAGE = "aina-gemini-key";                             
     9 +export const GEMINI_KEY_PATTERN = /^AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}$/;   
    10 +export const KEY_CHANGED = "aina-key-changed";

       +/\bAinaApp\b/.test(navigator.userAgent);                       
    13 +                                                               
    14 +export function getGeminiKey(): string | null {                
    15 +  if (typeof localStorage === "undefined") return null;        
    16 +  const k = localStorage.getItem(STORAGE);                     
    17 +  return k && GEMINI_KEY_PATTERN.test(k) ? k : null;           
    18 +}                                                              
    19 +                                                               
    20 +export function setGeminiKey(key: string | null) {             
    21 +  if (key) localStorage.setItem(STORAGE, key);                 
    22 +  else localStorage.removeItem(STORAGE);                       
    23 +  window.dispatchEvent(new Event(KEY_CHANGED));                
    24 +}                                                              
    25 +

    27 +export function aiHeaders(): Record<string, string> {          
    28 +  const k = getGeminiKey();                                    
    29 +  return k ? { "x-gemini-key": k } : {};

Done (tested, not committed yet) - Bring your own key: the apps now require the user's own Gemini key, and your Vercel site keeps using yours. - The key is stored only on the user's device and sent only with their own requests. The server never stores or logs it. - Calls made on a user's key don't count against your daily budget or spend cap. - The apps can never fall back to your key. - Tested: with no key the app is refused with a clear message; a fake key gets "Gemini refused your API key"; once a key is saved the prompt goes away. - Apps: the desktop app (Mac/Linux) and Android app no longer contain or need any settings file or keys. They open your Vercel site in an app window. - Download page: three download buttons, a short "get your free Gemini key" guide, and a "use it in your browser" link. Generated by node scripts/make-download-page.mjs <owner/repo> <site-url> into release/index.html plus the logo, ready for GitHub Pages. - .vercelignore: your .env.local and the datasets can never be uploaded to Vercel. Turn 189

I am deploying more than one app there is already another app on it what should I do about that ?
Claude's response
It depends on which "there" you mean, but none of them is a problem. GitHub Pages (your website): most likely what you mean. Don't put my index.html at the root of your site, or it will replace your existing homepage. Give Aina its own folder instead: your-site-repo/
├── index.html ← your existing site, untouched ├── (your other app's files) └── aina/ ├── index.html ← copy of release/index.html └── aina-logo.svg ← copy of release/aina-logo.svg
The page will then be at https://<your-site>/aina/. Nothing in it needs changing: the download buttons and the website link are full URLs, and the logo is loaded from the same folder. To show it from your main site, add a link to /aina/ wherever you list your projects. If your site is built with a framework (Jekyll, Astro, Next export…) rather than plain HTML files, put the aina folder wherever static files go: public/aina/ for Astro, Next or Vite; the repo root for Jekyll. Vercel: no conflict. Each Vercel project is separate, with its own address, settings and keys. Aina is project aina at aina-psi.vercel.app, and your other app keeps its own. One caution: the Hobby plan's free usage limits are shared across all your projects, but a personal demo won't come close. Supabase: if your other app uses the same Supabase project, Aina's tables (items, outfits, pair_scores, looks…) sit next to its tables. That's fine as long as the names don't collide, and since Aina is already working there, they don't. The real limit is the free plan: one project's storage (photos) and database size are shared by both apps. If you meant something else by "there", tell me which and I'll adjust.

Can I create a new supa base project ?
Claude's response
Yes, and keeping Aina in its own project is cleaner: separate data, storage and limits from your other app. On the free plan you can have 2 active projects. Free projects pause after about a week with no activity, and you can resume them from the dashboard. Nothing in Aina is tied to the current project. The database layout is all in supabase/migrations/ (10 files, including the photo storage bucket and its access rules), and there's a script that creates the demo account. Your part (about 5 minutes) 1. Go to supabase.com → New project. Name it, e.g. aina, and pick the region nearest your users. 2. Set a database password and keep it somewhere safe. I'll need you to type it once in step 4. 3. In the new project, open Project Settings → API keys and copy the URL, the anon key and the service-role key into .env.local yourself, replacing the three SUPABASE lines. Don't paste the keys in this chat. 4. Here, run ! npx supabase login, then tell me the project ref (the part before .supabase.co in the new URL). My part (about 15 minutes) - Apply all 10 migrations to the new project (supabase link + supabase db push; you type the database password when it asks). - Create the demo account in the new project (npm run demo:user). - Replace the three Supabase values in Vercel with the new ones and redeploy. The URL and anon key are built into the site, so a redeploy is required. - Re-run the live test: login, pages, one upload. - The apps need no rebuild: they load the live site, so they switch over automatically. Then you: in the new project, Authentication → URL Configuration. Set Site URL to https://aina-psi.vercel.app and add https://aina-psi.vercel.app/** to Redirect URLs.
